title: 4  Brownian motion and stochastic calculus
text:
4.4 The Itô integral

\(L^2\) is the space of random variables with \(\mathbb E[X^2] < \infty\), with norm \(\|X\| = \mathbb E[X^2]^{1/2}\). \(X_n \to X\) in \(L^2\) (in mean square) if \(\|X_n - X\| \to 0\). \(L^2\) is complete: every Cauchy sequence converges to a unique limit. Moreover, \(L^2\) limits of Gaussian random variables are Gaussian, and \(L^2\) convergence implies \(\mathbb E[X_n^2] \to \mathbb E[X^2]\) and \(\mathbb E[X_n\mid\mathcal G] \to \mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]\) in \(L^2\) for any \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal G\).

The plan: define \(\int_0^T\beta_u\,dW_u\) for simple integrands, prove its properties, then extend by approximation. Integrands are always adapted.
Step 0. For a deterministic indicator \(\beta_t = c\,\mathbf 1_{[a,b)}(t)\) the only reasonable definition is \(\int_0^T\beta_u\,dW_u = c(W_b - W_a)\).

\(\beta\) is simple if there are times \(0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_n = T\) such that \[\beta_t = \sum_{i=1}^n\beta_{t_{i-1}}\mathbf 1_{[t_{i-1}, t_i)}(t),\] with each \(\beta_{t_{i-1}}\) square-integrable and \(\mathcal F_{t_{i-1}}\)-measurable: a piecewise-constant function of time with random heights. Its stochastic integral is \[\int_0^T\beta_u\,dW_u := \sum_{i=1}^n\beta_{t_{i-1}}\bigl(W_{t_i} - W_{t_{i-1}}\bigr),\] and \(\int_0^t\beta_u\,dW_u = \sum_i\beta_{t_{i-1}}(W_{t_i\wedge t} - W_{t_{i-1}\wedge t})\) for \(t \leq T\).


Figure: a simple integrand — constant on each interval, with a random height known at the left endpoint.
It is essential that the integrand is evaluated at the left endpoint of each interval, against the forward increment of \(W\): the height is decided before the noise of that interval is revealed. (In finance: you choose your portfolio before prices move.)

For simple \(\beta\):

Linearity: \(\int(\beta + \gamma)\,dW = \int\beta\,dW + \int\gamma\,dW\).
Martingale property: \(\mathbb E\bigl[\int_0^t\beta_u\,dW_u\bigm|\mathcal F_s\bigr] = \int_0^s\beta_u\,dW_u\) for \(s \leq t\); in particular \(\mathbb E\bigl[\int_0^T\beta_u\,dW_u\bigr] = 0\).
Itô isometry: \(\mathbb E\Bigl[\bigl(\int_0^T\beta_u\,dW_u\bigr)^2\Bigr] = \mathbb E\Bigl[\int_0^T\beta_u^2\,du\Bigr]\); hence \(\mathrm{Var}\bigl(\int_0^T\beta_u\,dW_u\bigr) = \mathbb E\bigl[\int_0^T\beta_u^2\,du\bigr]\).
If \(\beta\) is deterministic, \(\int_0^T\beta_u\,dW_u \sim \mathcal N\bigl(0, \int_0^T\beta_u^2\,du\bigr)\).


Proof of 2. Each term contributes \(\beta_{t_{i-1}}(W_{t_i\wedge t} - W_{t_{i-1}\wedge t})\). Terms entirely before \(s\) are \(\mathcal F_s\)-measurable and stay. For the interval \([t_j, t_{j+1})\) containing \(s\), \(\beta_{t_j}\) is \(\mathcal F_s\)-measurable and \(\mathbb E[W_{t_{j+1}\wedge t}\mid\mathcal F_s] = W_s\), giving \(\beta_{t_j}(W_s - W_{t_j})\). For later intervals, condition first on \(\mathcal F_{t_{i-1}} \supseteq \mathcal F_s\): \(\mathbb E\bigl[\beta_{t_{i-1}}(W_{t_i\wedge t} - W_{t_{i-1}\wedge t})\bigm|\mathcal F_{t_{i-1}}\bigr] = \beta_{t_{i-1}}\cdot 0\), and the tower rule kills them. What remains is exactly \(\int_0^s\beta_u\,dW_u\).
Proof of 3. Expand the square: \(\sum_i\beta_{t_{i-1}}^2(\Delta W_i)^2 + 2\sum_{i<j}\beta_{t_{i-1}}\beta_{t_{j-1}}\Delta W_i\,\Delta W_j\). For the diagonal terms, conditioning on \(\mathcal F_{t_{i-1}}\), \(\mathbb E[\beta_{t_{i-1}}^2(\Delta W_i)^2] = \mathbb E[\beta_{t_{i-1}}^2]\,(t_i - t_{i-1})\), whose sum is \(\mathbb E\int_0^T\beta_u^2\,du\). For \(i < j\) everything but \(\Delta W_j\) is \(\mathcal F_{t_{j-1}}\)-measurable and \(\mathbb E[\Delta W_j\mid\mathcal F_{t_{j-1}}] = 0\), so cross terms vanish.
Proof of 4. The integral is a finite sum of independent Gaussians \(\beta_{t_{i-1}}\Delta W_i \sim \mathcal N(0, \beta_{t_{i-1}}^2(t_i - t_{i-1}))\). \(\square\)

An adapted process \(\beta\) is integrable if \(\|\beta\|_T^2 := \mathbb E\bigl[\int_0^T\beta_u^2\,du\bigr] < \infty\). (\(\|\cdot\|_T\) is a norm on processes and satisfies the triangle inequality.)


If \(\beta\) is integrable, there exist simple processes \(\beta_n\) with \(\|\beta - \beta_n\|_T \to 0\). The integrals \(X_n = \int_0^T\beta_{n,u}\,dW_u\) form a Cauchy sequence in \(L^2\), and \(\int_0^T\beta_u\,dW_u\) is defined as their \(L^2\) limit, which does not depend on the approximating sequence.

Proof. \((\beta_n)\) is Cauchy for \(\|\cdot\|_T\): \(\|\beta_m - \beta_n\|_T \leq \|\beta_m - \beta\|_T + \|\beta - \beta_n\|_T\). By linearity and the Itô isometry for simple processes, \[\|X_m - X_n\|_{L^2} = \Bigl\|\int_0^T(\beta_{m,u} - \beta_{n,u})\,dW_u\Bigr\|_{L^2} = \|\beta_m - \beta_n\|_T,\] so \((X_n)\) is Cauchy in \(L^2\), and completeness gives a unique limit. \(\square\)
The limit is a random variable, not built path by path; letting the upper limit vary gives the stochastic integral process \(\bigl(\int_0^t\beta_u\,dW_u\bigr)_{t\in[0,T]}\). All four properties pass to the limit: the Itô isometry because \(L^2\) convergence implies convergence of second moments; the martingale property because conditional expectations converge in \(L^2\) and limits are unique; Gaussianity for deterministic integrands because \(L^2\) limits of Gaussians are Gaussian.






Executive summary. For an adapted \(\beta\) with \(\mathbb E\int_0^T\beta_u^2\,du < \infty\): the Itô integral exists; \(\bigl(\int_0^t\beta_u\,dW_u\bigr)_t\) is a martingale with zero mean; its variance is \(\mathbb E\int_0^T\beta_u^2\,du\) (Itô isometry); for deterministic \(\beta\) it is Gaussian.

4.5 Stochastic differential equations
We can now make sense of \[X_t = x + \int_0^t\alpha(u, X_u)\,du + \int_0^t\beta(u, X_u)\,dW_u, \qquad t \in [0, T],\] written in short-hand as the stochastic differential equation (SDE) \[dX_t = \alpha(t, X_t)\,dt + \beta(t, X_t)\,dW_t, \qquad X_0 = x .\] \(\alpha\) is the drift and \(\beta\) the diffusion (volatility) coefficient. If \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are Lipschitz in \(x\) with linear growth, a unique solution exists (and in many more general cases); the solution is a Markov process.

title: 4  Brownian motion and stochastic calculus
text:
4.6 Quadratic variation
For a partition \(\pi = \{0 = t_0 < \dots < t_n = t\}\) with mesh \(|\pi| = \max_i(t_i - t_{i-1})\), define \[[W]_t := \lim_{|\pi|\to0}\sum_{i=1}^n(W_{t_i} - W_{t_{i-1}})^2 \qquad\text{(limit in } L^2).\]

\([W]_t = t\) for every \(t \geq 0\).

Proof. Write \(\Delta W_i = W_{t_i} - W_{t_{i-1}}\), \(\Delta t_i = t_i - t_{i-1}\) and \(Z_i = \Delta W_i/\sqrt{\Delta t_i}\), i.i.d. \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). Then \(\sum_i(\Delta W_i)^2 - t = \sum_i\Delta t_i(Z_i^2 - 1)\), a sum of independent zero-mean terms, so \[\Bigl\|\sum_i(\Delta W_i)^2 - t\Bigr\|_{L^2}^2 = \sum_i\Delta t_i^2\,\mathbb E[(Z_i^2 - 1)^2] = 2\sum_i\Delta t_i^2 \leq 2|\pi|\sum_i\Delta t_i = 2|\pi|t \to 0. \qquad\square\]
Note that \([W]_t = t = \mathrm{Var}(W_t)\). Locally: \(\mathbb E[(\Delta W_t)^2] = \Delta t\) while \(\mathrm{Var}((\Delta W_t)^2) = 2\Delta t^2\), so as \(\Delta t \to 0\) the squared increment becomes deterministic, \((\Delta W_t)^2 \approx \Delta t\). In differential form, \[d[W]_t = dt, \qquad (dW_t)^2 = dt .\]

Brownian paths have infinite first variation \(V_W(t) = \sup_\pi\sum_i|W_{t_i} - W_{t_{i-1}}|\) on every interval \([0, t]\).

Proof. \(\sum_i(\Delta W_i)^2 \leq \max_i|\Delta W_i|\,\sum_i|\Delta W_i| \leq \max_i|\Delta W_i|\,V_W(t)\). As \(|\pi| \to 0\) the left side tends to \(t > 0\), while \(\max_i|\Delta W_i| \to 0\) by continuity of the path. This forces \(V_W(t) = +\infty\). \(\square\)
(For a \(C^1\) function \(f\), \(V_f(t) = \int_0^t|f'(u)|\,du < \infty\) and its quadratic variation is zero.)

title: 4  Brownian motion and stochastic calculus
text:
4.7 Itô’s formula
If \(X\) solves an SDE, what SDE does \(f(t, X_t)\) solve? Write \(f_t, f_x, f_{xx}\) for the partial derivatives.

Let \(f \in C^{1,2}([0,T]\times\mathbb R)\) and \(dX_t = \alpha(t, X_t)\,dt + \beta(t, X_t)\,dW_t\). Then \[df(t, X_t) = \Bigl(f_t + \alpha f_x + \frac12\beta^2f_{xx}\Bigr)(t, X_t)\,dt + \beta(t, X_t)\,f_x(t, X_t)\,dW_t .\]

The extra term \(\tfrac12\beta^2f_{xx}\), the Itô correction, is absent from ordinary calculus. It exists because Brownian motion has non-zero quadratic variation.
Heuristic derivation. Over \([t, t + \Delta t]\), \(\Delta X \approx \alpha\Delta t + \beta\Delta W\). A second-order Taylor expansion gives \[f(t + \Delta t, X_t + \Delta X) - f(t, X_t) \approx f_t\Delta t + f_x\Delta X + \tfrac12f_{tt}\Delta t^2 + \tfrac12f_{xx}(\Delta X)^2 + f_{tx}\Delta t\,\Delta X .\] Substituting \(\Delta X\): \((\Delta X)^2 = \alpha^2\Delta t^2 + 2\alpha\beta\Delta t\,\Delta W + \beta^2(\Delta W)^2\). All terms of order higher than \(\Delta t\) — \(\Delta t^2\), \(\Delta t\,\Delta W \sim \Delta t^{3/2}\) — vanish in the limit, but \((\Delta W)^2 \approx \Delta t\) does not: it contributes \(\tfrac12f_{xx}\beta^2\Delta t\). Keeping the first-order terms gives the formula. The rigorous proof makes this precise with the quadratic variation. A convenient mnemonic is the multiplication table \(dt\cdot dt = 0\), \(dt\cdot dW_t = 0\), \(dW_t\cdot dW_t = dt\).

With \(f(t, x) = tx\) and \(X = W\): \(f_t = x\), \(f_x = t\), \(f_{xx} = 0\), so \(d(tW_t) = W_t\,dt + t\,dW_t\), i.e. \(\int_0^ts\,dW_s = tW_t - \int_0^tW_s\,ds\). With \(f(x) = x^2\): \(d(W_t^2) = dt + 2W_t\,dW_t\), i.e. \(\int_0^tW_s\,dW_s = \tfrac12(W_t^2 - t)\) — not \(\tfrac12W_t^2\) as ordinary calculus would suggest.

title: 4  Brownian motion and stochastic calculus
text:
4.8 Geometric Brownian motion

The SDE \[dX_t = \mu X_t\,dt + \sigma X_t\,dW_t, \qquad X_0 = x_0 > 0,\] with drift \(\mu\) and volatility \(\sigma > 0\) defines geometric Brownian motion (GBM). It is the case \(\alpha(t, x) = \mu x\), \(\beta(t, x) = \sigma x\) of the general SDE, and the starting point of the Black–Scholes model.


\[X_t = x_0\exp\Bigl(\Bigl(\mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Bigr)t + \sigma W_t\Bigr), \qquad t \geq 0.\]

First derivation (separation of variables). Since the solution is Markov, look for \(X_t = f(t, W_t)\) with \(f(t, x) = g(t)h(x)\). Itô’s formula with \(X = W\) gives \[dX_t = \Bigl(g'(t)h(W_t) + \tfrac12g(t)h''(W_t)\Bigr)dt + g(t)h'(W_t)\,dW_t .\] Matching with \(dX_t = \mu g h\,dt + \sigma gh\,dW_t\): the \(dW_t\) terms give \(h' = \sigma h\), so \(h(x) = e^{\sigma x}\); the \(dt\) terms give \(g' + \tfrac12\sigma^2g = \mu g\), so \(g(t) = g(0)e^{(\mu - \sigma^2/2)t}\); and \(g(0) = x_0\).
Second derivation (logarithm). If \(X > 0\), set \(Y_t = \log X_t\). Itô’s formula with \(f(x) = \log x\) (\(f' = 1/x\), \(f'' = -1/x^2\)): \[dY_t = \frac{1}{X_t}dX_t - \frac{1}{2X_t^2}\sigma^2X_t^2\,dt = \Bigl(\mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Bigr)dt + \sigma\,dW_t,\] which integrates directly: \(Y_t = \log x_0 + (\mu - \sigma^2/2)t + \sigma W_t\). \(\square\)
Consequences: \(X_t > 0\); \(\log X_t \sim \mathcal N\bigl(\log x_0 + (\mu - \sigma^2/2)t, \sigma^2t\bigr)\), i.e. \(X_t\) is log-normal; and \(\mathbb E[X_t] = x_0e^{\mu t}\) (by the exponential martingale), so \(\mu\) is the expected growth rate. The term \(-\sigma^2/2\) in the exponent is the Itô correction: the median grows at rate \(\mu - \sigma^2/2 < \mu\).

4.9 Diffusions and partial differential equations
Itô’s formula connects SDEs with PDEs; this connection is the bridge between the probabilistic (expectation) and analytic (PDE) views of pricing used from Chapter 5 on.

If \(dX_t = \mu_t\,dt + \sigma_t\,dW_t\) with \(\mathbb E\int_0^T\sigma_t^2dt < \infty\), then \(X\) is a martingale iff \(\mu_t = 0\) (a.s., for a.e. \(t\)); if \(\mu_t \geq 0\) it is a submartingale.

Proof. \(X_t - X_s = \int_s^t\mu_u\,du + \int_s^t\sigma_u\,dW_u\); the stochastic integral has zero conditional expectation, so \(\mathbb E[X_t - X_s\mid\mathcal F_s] = \mathbb E[\int_s^t\mu_u\,du\mid\mathcal F_s]\), which is zero for all \(s < t\) iff \(\mu = 0\), and non-negative if \(\mu \geq 0\). \(\square\)
Consider a diffusion \(dX_s = \mu(s, X_s)\,ds + \sigma(s, X_s)\,dW_s\) started at \(X_t = x\), and its infinitesimal generator \[\mathcal A F(t, x) = \mu(t, x)\,F_x(t, x) + \tfrac12\sigma^2(t, x)\,F_{xx}(t, x).\] By Itô’s formula \(dF(s, X_s) = (F_t + \mathcal AF)(s, X_s)\,ds + \sigma F_x\,dW_s\).

Let \(F\) solve the boundary-value problem \[F_t + \mathcal AF - r(t, x)F = 0, \qquad F(T, x) = \Phi(x).\] Under integrability conditions, \[F(t, x) = \mathbb E_{t,x}\Bigl[e^{-\int_t^Tr(s, X_s)\,ds}\,\Phi(X_T)\Bigr],\] where \(\mathbb E_{t,x}\) denotes expectation for the diffusion started at \(X_t = x\). With a source term, \(F_t + \mathcal AF + k = 0\) and \(F(T, \cdot) = \Phi\) (and \(r = 0\)), \(F(t, x) = \mathbb E_{t,x}[\Phi(X_T)] + \int_t^T\mathbb E_{t,x}[k(s, X_s)]\,ds\).

Proof. Apply Itô’s formula to \(Z_s = e^{-\int_t^sr(u, X_u)du}F(s, X_s)\) on \([t, T]\): the \(ds\)-term is \(e^{-\int r}(F_t + \mathcal AF - rF) = 0\), so \(Z\) is a martingale (given integrability), and \(F(t, x) = Z_t = \mathbb E_{t,x}[Z_T]\). For the source term, \(F(T, X_T) - F(t, x) = -\int_t^Tk\,ds + \int_t^T\sigma F_x\,dW\); take expectations. \(\square\)
The Black–Scholes PDE is the case \(\mu = rx\), \(\sigma(x) = \sigma x\), constant \(r\). Two further PDEs describe the transition density \(p(s, y; t, x)\) of \(X_t\) given \(X_s = y\):

Kolmogorov backward equation (in the initial variables): \(\partial_sp + \mu(s, y)\partial_yp + \tfrac12\sigma^2(s, y)\partial_{yy}p = 0\), with \(p(s, \cdot; t, x) \to \delta_x\) as \(s \to t\). It is Feynman–Kač with \(\Phi = \delta_x\).
Kolmogorov forward (Fokker–Planck) equation (in the final variables): \(\partial_tp = -\partial_x\bigl(\mu(t, x)p\bigr) + \tfrac12\partial_{xx}\bigl(\sigma^2(t, x)p\bigr)\), with \(p \to \delta_y\) as \(t \to s\). It follows from \(\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb E[h(X_t)] = \mathbb E[\mathcal Ah(X_t)]\) for test functions \(h\), after integrating by parts.

For Brownian motion with drift (\(\mu = \alpha\), \(\sigma\) constant) the solution is the Gaussian kernel \(p = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2(t-s)}}\exp\bigl(-\frac{(x - y - \alpha(t-s))^2}{2\sigma^2(t-s)}\bigr)\); Dupire’s equation of Chapter 7 is a forward equation for call prices.

4.10 Exercises
Problems from Björk (B), Chapters 4–5.

(B 4.1) Compute \(dZ\) for (a) \(Z_t = e^{\alpha t}\); (b) \(Z_t = \int_0^tg_s\,dW_s\) with \(g\) adapted; (c) \(Z_t = e^{\alpha W_t}\); (d) \(Z_t = e^{\alpha X_t}\) with \(dX = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dW\); (e) \(Z_t = X_t^2\) with \(dX = \alpha X\,dt + \sigma X\,dW\).


Solution. 

\(dZ = \alpha Z\,dt\). (b) \(dZ = g_t\,dW_t\). (c) \(dZ = \tfrac12\alpha^2Z\,dt + \alpha Z\,dW\). (d) \(dZ = Z\bigl(\alpha\mu + \tfrac12\alpha^2\sigma^2\bigr)dt + \alpha\sigma Z\,dW\). (e) \(dZ = 2X\,dX + (dX)^2 = (2\alpha + \sigma^2)Z\,dt + 2\sigma Z\,dW\): the square of a GBM is a GBM.



(B 4.2) If \(dX = \alpha X\,dt + \sigma X\,dW\), find the SDE satisfied by \(Z = 1/X\).


Solution. With \(f(x) = 1/x\), \(f' = -1/x^2\), \(f'' = 2/x^3\): \(dZ = -\frac{dX}{X^2} + \frac{\sigma^2X^2}{X^3}dt = (\sigma^2 - \alpha)Z\,dt - \sigma Z\,dW\). \(Z\) is again a GBM — relevant for exchange rates, where \(1/S\) is the rate quoted the other way round.


(B 4.3) Let \(X_t = \int_0^t\sigma(s)\,dW_s\) with \(\sigma\) deterministic. Using Itô’s formula on \(e^{iuX_t}\), show that \(\mathbb E[e^{iuX_t}] = \exp\bigl(-\tfrac{u^2}{2}\int_0^t\sigma^2(s)\,ds\bigr)\), so that \(X_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \int_0^t\sigma^2)\).


Solution. \(d e^{iuX} = iue^{iuX}\sigma\,dW - \tfrac12u^2\sigma^2e^{iuX}dt\). Taking expectations, \(m(t) = \mathbb E[e^{iuX_t}]\) satisfies \(m' = -\tfrac12u^2\sigma^2(t)m\), \(m(0) = 1\), so \(m(t) = \exp(-\tfrac{u^2}{2}\int_0^t\sigma^2)\), the characteristic function of the stated Gaussian.


(B 4.7) Let \(W^1, W^2\) be independent Brownian motions and \(Q_n = \sum_{k=1}^n\Delta W^1_k\,\Delta W^2_k\) on an equidistant partition of \([0, t]\). Show that \(Q_n \to 0\) in \(L^2\), justifying \(dW^1\,dW^2 = 0\).


Solution. The products are independent with mean \(0\) and variance \(\mathbb E[(\Delta W^1)^2]\mathbb E[(\Delta W^2)^2] = (t/n)^2\). Hence \(\mathbb E[Q_n] = 0\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(Q_n) = n(t/n)^2 = t^2/n \to 0\).


(B 5.5) If \(dX = \alpha X\,dt + \sigma X\,dW\) and \(Y = X^\beta\), show that \(Y\) is a GBM and identify its drift and volatility.


Solution. \(dY = \beta X^{\beta-1}dX + \tfrac12\beta(\beta - 1)X^{\beta-2}\sigma^2X^2dt = Y\bigl(\beta\alpha + \tfrac12\beta(\beta-1)\sigma^2\bigr)dt + \beta\sigma Y\,dW\).


(B 5.1) Show that \(X_t = e^{\alpha t}x_0 + \sigma\int_0^te^{\alpha(t-s)}dW_s\) solves \(dX = \alpha X\,dt + \sigma\,dW\), \(X_0 = x_0\), and find its mean and variance.


Solution. Write \(X_t = e^{\alpha t}(x_0 + \sigma R_t)\) with \(R_t = \int_0^te^{-\alpha s}dW_s\). By the product rule, \(dX = \alpha X\,dt + e^{\alpha t}\sigma e^{-\alpha t}dW = \alpha X\,dt + \sigma\,dW\). Mean \(e^{\alpha t}x_0\); variance \(\sigma^2\int_0^te^{2\alpha(t-s)}ds = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\alpha}(e^{2\alpha t} - 1)\). For \(\alpha = -\kappa < 0\) this is the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, with stationary variance \(\sigma^2/(2\kappa)\).


(B 5.11) Solve \(F_t + \tfrac12x^2F_{xx} + x = 0\), \(F(T, x) = \log(x^2)\).


Solution. Feynman–Kač with source \(k = x\) and the diffusion \(dX = X\,dW\), so \(X_s = x\exp(W_s - W_t - (s - t)/2)\) and \(\mathbb E_{t,x}[X_s] = x\). Then \(\mathbb E_{t,x}[\log X_T^2] = 2\log x - (T - t)\) and \[F(t, x) = \log x^2 - (T - t) + x(T - t).\] Check: \(F_t = 1 - x\), \(\tfrac12x^2F_{xx} = \tfrac12x^2(-2/x^2) = -1\), and \(1 - x - 1 + x = 0\). ✓


(B 5.15) For \(dX = \alpha\,dt + \sigma\,dW\), compute the transition density \(p(s, y; t, x)\) and verify the Fokker–Planck equation.


Solution. \(X_t = y + \alpha(t - s) + \sigma(W_t - W_s)\), Gaussian: \(p = (2\pi\sigma^2\tau)^{-1/2}e^{-(x - y - \alpha\tau)^2/(2\sigma^2\tau)}\), \(\tau = t - s\). With \(z = x - y - \alpha\tau\): \(\partial_xp = -\frac{z}{\sigma^2\tau}p\), \(\partial_{xx}p = \bigl(\frac{z^2}{\sigma^4\tau^2} - \frac{1}{\sigma^2\tau}\bigr)p\), \(\partial_tp = \bigl(-\frac{1}{2\tau} + \frac{z^2}{2\sigma^2\tau^2} + \frac{\alpha z}{\sigma^2\tau}\bigr)p\), and indeed \(\partial_tp = -\alpha\,\partial_xp + \tfrac12\sigma^2\partial_{xx}p\).

title: 5  The Black–Scholes–Merton model
text:
5.1 The market
The Black–Scholes–Merton (BSM) model, published in 1973 by Black and Scholes and by Merton (Nobel prize 1997 to Scholes and Merton), is the most successful stochastic model of a financial market (“imagination creates reality”, Wagner). It is the continuous-time limit of the binomial model, and the same logic applies: replicate the derivative with a self-financing portfolio, and its price follows by no arbitrage. This chapter derives the hedge, the Black–Scholes PDE, its probabilistic solution through the Feynman–Kač formula and the risk-neutral probability, and the explicit formula for calls and puts. It then turns to practice: numerical methods, historical and implied volatility, the Greeks, discrete hedging errors, Delta–Gamma hedging, and the model’s limitations.
Trading takes place continuously over \([0, T]\). Two assets are traded:
\(S\) is a Markov process and \(S_t\) is log-normal with \(\mathbb E[S_t] = se^{\mu t}\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(S_t) = s^2e^{2\mu t}(e^{\sigma^2t} - 1)\).

text:

a stock (paying no dividends) following a geometric Brownian motion, \[dS_t = \mu S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t, \qquad S_0 = s > 0, \qquad S_t = s\exp\Bigl(\Bigl(\mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\Bigr)t + \sigma W_t\Bigr),\] with drift \(\mu\) (the expected rate of return) and volatility \(\sigma > 0\).

title: 5  The Black–Scholes–Merton model
text:
5.2 Self-financing strategies

A dynamic portfolio is a pair \(\theta = (\theta^B, \theta^S)\) of adapted processes: \(\theta^B_t\) and \(\theta^S_t\) are the units of bank account and stock held over \([t, t + dt]\). Its value is \(V_t(\theta) = \theta^B_tB_t + \theta^S_tS_t\).

In the multi-period binomial model the self-financing condition \(\theta^B_tB_{t+1} + \theta^S_tS_{t+1} = \theta^B_{t+1}B_{t+1} + \theta^S_{t+1}S_{t+1}\) implies \[\Delta V_{t+1} = V_{t+1} - V_t = \theta^B_t\,\Delta B_{t+1} + \theta^S_t\,\Delta S_{t+1}:\] the value changes only through price changes, never through injections or withdrawals of money. Letting the time step go to zero motivates:

\(\theta\) is self-financing if \[V_t(\theta) = V_0(\theta) + \int_0^t\theta^B_u\,dB_u + \int_0^t\theta^S_u\,dS_u, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad dV_t(\theta) = \theta^B_t\,dB_t + \theta^S_t\,dS_t .\]

Substituting the dynamics, \(dV_t = (\theta^B_trB_t + \theta^S_t\mu S_t)\,dt + \theta^S_t\sigma S_t\,dW_t\). The last term is a stochastic integral, so we require \(\mathbb E\int_0^T(\theta^S_tS_t)^2\,dt < \infty\).
An arbitrage is a self-financing \(\theta\) with \(V_0(\theta) = 0\), \(V_T(\theta) \geq 0\) a.s. and \(\mathbb P(V_T(\theta) > 0) > 0\). The BSM model is free of arbitrage for all values of \(r\), \(\mu\), \(\sigma\), provided strategies are restricted to a suitable class (excluding, for instance, “doubling strategies”); this follows from the existence of the risk-neutral probability below.

title: 5  The Black–Scholes–Merton model
text:
5.3 Hedging and the Black–Scholes PDE
Consider a European, path-independent derivative with payoff \(G(S_T)\). Since \(S\) is Markov, it is natural to look for its price in the form \(\Pi_t(G) = F(t, S_t)\) for a pricing function \(F : [0, T]\times(0, \infty) \to \mathbb R\): derivatives are priced relative to their underlying.

Let \(F \in C^{1,2}\) satisfy \(F(T, x) = G(x)\). The self-financing portfolio \[\theta^S_t = F_x(t, S_t), \qquad \theta^B_t = \frac{F_t(t, S_t) + \tfrac12\sigma^2S_t^2F_{xx}(t, S_t)}{rB_t},\] started from \(V_0(\theta) = F(0, s)\), has \(dV_t(\theta) = dF(t, S_t)\); hence \(V_T(\theta) = G(S_T)\) almost surely.

Derivation. For a self-financing \(\theta\), \[dV_t = (\theta^B_trB_t + \theta^S_t\mu S_t)\,dt + \theta^S_t\sigma S_t\,dW_t. \tag{1}\] By Itô’s formula, \[dF(t, S_t) = \Bigl(F_t + \mu S_tF_x + \tfrac12\sigma^2S_t^2F_{xx}\Bigr)dt + \sigma S_tF_x\,dW_t. \tag{2}\] Matching the \(dW_t\) terms of (1) and (2) gives \(\theta^S_t = F_x(t, S_t)\). Matching the \(dt\) terms with this choice, the \(\mu\)-terms cancel and \(\theta^B_trB_t = F_t + \tfrac12\sigma^2S_t^2F_{xx}\). If \(dV_t = dF(t, S_t)\) and \(V_0 = F(0, s)\), then \(V_T = F(T, S_T) = G(S_T)\). \(\square\)
\(\theta^S_t = F_x(t, S_t)\) is the Delta of the derivative: exactly as in the binomial model, holding \(\Delta\) shares offsets a short position in the derivative.
By the law of one price, \(F(t, S_t) = V_t(\theta) = \theta^B_tB_t + \theta^S_tS_t\). Substituting the hedge, \[F(t, S_t) = \frac{F_t + \tfrac12\sigma^2S_t^2F_{xx}}{r} + F_xS_t,\] which must hold with probability one, i.e. for every possible value of \(S_t\) — every \(x \in (0, \infty)\).

Under no arbitrage, the pricing function of the derivative with payoff \(G(S_T)\) solves \[F_t(t, x) + rxF_x(t, x) + \frac12\sigma^2x^2F_{xx}(t, x) - rF(t, x) = 0, \qquad (t, x) \in [0, T)\times(0, \infty),\] \[F(T, x) = G(x), \qquad x \in (0, \infty).\]

The pricing problem has become a deterministic one: randomness has disappeared. Some PDEs can be solved explicitly; otherwise numerical schemes apply.






The drift \(\mu\) does not appear in the PDE. The arbitrage-free price does not depend on the expected return of the stock — the continuous-time analogue of the irrelevance of \(p_u, p_d\) in the binomial model. Hence the price would be the same if \(\mu\) were replaced by \(r\), i.e. in a world where investors are risk-neutral, where prices are discounted expectations. This is risk-neutral valuation.

title: 5  The Black–Scholes–Merton model
section: 5.4 The Feynman–Kač formula and the risk-neutral probability
text:
5.4 The Feynman–Kač formula and the risk-neutral probability

Let \(F \in C^{1,2}\) solve the Black–Scholes PDE with terminal condition \(G\). Under suitable integrability conditions, \[F(t, S_t) = e^{-r(T-t)}\,\mathbb E^Q\bigl[G(S_T)\bigm|S_t\bigr],\] where \(Q\) is a probability under which \[dS_t = rS_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW^Q_t\] with \(W^Q\) a \(Q\)-Brownian motion. In particular, the price today is \(F(0, s) = e^{-rT}\mathbb E^Q[G(S_T)]\).

Proof. Under \(Q\), consider \(Y_t = e^{-rt}F(t, S_t) = f(t, S_t)\) with \(f(t, x) = e^{-rt}F(t, x)\). By Itô’s formula, with \(f_t = -re^{-rt}F + e^{-rt}F_t\), \(f_x = e^{-rt}F_x\), \(f_{xx} = e^{-rt}F_{xx}\), \[dY_t = e^{-rt}\Bigl(F_t + rS_tF_x + \tfrac12\sigma^2S_t^2F_{xx} - rF\Bigr)dt + e^{-rt}\sigma S_tF_x\,dW^Q_t = e^{-rt}\sigma S_tF_x(t, S_t)\,dW^Q_t,\] since \(F\) solves the PDE. So \(Y_t = Y_0 + \int_0^te^{-ru}\sigma S_uF_x(u, S_u)\,dW^Q_u\); if \(\mathbb E^Q\int_0^Te^{-2ru}(\sigma S_uF_x)^2du < \infty\), the stochastic integral is a \(Q\)-martingale and \[e^{-rt}F(t, S_t) = Y_t = \mathbb E^Q[Y_T\mid\mathcal F_t] = e^{-rT}\mathbb E^Q[G(S_T)\mid\mathcal F_t],\] using the terminal condition \(F(T, S_T) = G(S_T)\). By the Markov property, conditioning on \(\mathcal F_t\) is the same as conditioning on \(S_t\). \(\square\)
This is the risk-neutral valuation formula of the BSM model. The model is formulated under the real-world (statistical) probability \(\mathbb P\), where \(dS_t = \mu S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW_t\); under the risk-neutral probability \(Q\), \(dS_t = rS_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW^Q_t\). Equating the two, \[dW^Q_t = dW_t + \frac{\mu - r}{\sigma}\,dt .\] The quantity \(\lambda = \frac{\mu - r}{\sigma}\) is the market price of risk (analogous to the Sharpe ratio): passing from \(\mathbb P\) to \(Q\), the risk premium of the stock is absorbed into the Brownian motion. Girsanov’s theorem makes this rigorous: there is a probability \(Q\) equivalent to \(\mathbb P\) under which \(W_t + \lambda t\) is a Brownian motion. Under \(Q\) the discounted stock price \(e^{-rt}S_t\) is a martingale, and so is every discounted self-financing portfolio — the continuous-time version of the binomial martingale property and the source of absence of arbitrage.

title: 5  The Black–Scholes–Merton model
text:
5.5 The Black–Scholes formula

The price of a European call with strike \(K\) and maturity \(T\) is \[\Pi^{\mathrm{Call}}_t(K, T) = S_t\,\Phi(d_1) - Ke^{-r(T-t)}\,\Phi(d_2),\] \[d_1 = \frac{\log(S_t/K) + \bigl(r + \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\bigr)(T - t)}{\sigma\sqrt{T - t}}, \qquad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T - t},\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function.

Proof. Under \(Q\), \(S_T = S_t\exp\bigl((r - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2})(T - t) + \sigma(W^Q_T - W^Q_t)\bigr)\) and \(Z = (W^Q_T - W^Q_t)/\sqrt{T - t} \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) is independent of \(\mathcal F_t\). Split \[e^{-r(T-t)}\mathbb E^Q[(S_T - K)^+\mid S_t] = e^{-r(T-t)}\underbrace{\mathbb E^Q[S_T\mathbf 1_{\{S_T > K\}}\mid S_t]}_{B} - Ke^{-r(T-t)}\underbrace{\mathbb E^Q[\mathbf 1_{\{S_T > K\}}\mid S_t]}_{A}.\]
(A) \(S_T > K\) iff \(\log S_t + (r - \tfrac{\sigma^2}2)(T - t) + \sigma\sqrt{T - t}\,Z > \log K\), iff \(Z > -d_2\). Hence \(A = Q(Z > -d_2) = \Phi(d_2)\) by symmetry.
(B) With the same event, \[B = S_te^{r(T-t)}\int_{-d_2}^{\infty}e^{-\frac{\sigma^2}{2}(T-t) + \sigma\sqrt{T-t}\,z}\,\frac{e^{-z^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dz = S_te^{r(T-t)}\int_{-d_2}^{\infty}\frac{e^{-(z - \sigma\sqrt{T-t})^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,dz,\] by completing the square. Substituting \(y = z - \sigma\sqrt{T - t}\), the integral is \(Q(Z > -d_2 - \sigma\sqrt{T - t}) = \Phi(d_2 + \sigma\sqrt{T - t}) = \Phi(d_1)\). Putting the pieces together gives the formula. \(\square\)
Interpretation. \(\Phi(d_2) = Q(S_T > K)\) is the risk-neutral probability that the call is exercised; \(S_t\Phi(d_1)\) is the value at \(t\) of receiving one unit of the underlying at \(T\) on the event \(\{S_T > K\}\).

\[\Pi^{\mathrm{Put}}_t(K, T) = Ke^{-r(T-t)}\Phi(-d_2) - S_t\Phi(-d_1).\]

Proof. By put–call parity, \(\Pi^{\mathrm{Put}}_t = \Pi^{\mathrm{Call}}_t - S_t + Ke^{-r(T-t)} = Ke^{-r(T-t)}(1 - \Phi(d_2)) - S_t(1 - \Phi(d_1))\), and \(1 - \Phi(x) = \Phi(-x)\). \(\square\)

Figure: Black–Scholes call price (bold) as a function of the spot, with \(K = 100\), \(\sigma = 0.2\), \(r = 0\), \(T - t = 0.25\); grey: intrinsic value.
Moneyness. At time \(t\) a call is in the money if \(S_t > K\), out of the money if \(S_t < K\), at the money if \(S_t = K\).

The BS call price is

decreasing and convex in \(K\) (clear from \(e^{-r(T-t)}\mathbb E^Q[(S_T - K)^+]\));
increasing and convex in \(S_t\);
increasing in \(r\) (under \(Q\), \(r\) is the growth rate of the underlying and the discount rate of the strike);
increasing in \(\sigma\) (an option is a right: more dispersion raises the upside, while the downside is capped);
increasing in the maturity \(T\) (same intuition as volatility).

title: 5  The Black–Scholes–Merton model
section: 5.6 Extensions: dividends and other European claims
text:
5.6 Extensions: dividends and other European claims
Continuous dividend yield. If the stock pays dividends continuously at rate \(q\) (a good model for an index), the self-financing condition includes the dividends received, and under \(Q\) the total return — price change plus dividends — is \(r\): \[dS_t = (r - q)S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,dW^Q_t .\] Repeating the computation of the Black–Scholes formula with \(\mathbb E^Q[S_T] = S_te^{(r-q)\tau}\), \(\tau = T - t\), gives Merton’s formula \[\Pi^{\mathrm{Call}}_t = S_te^{-q\tau}\Phi(d_1) - Ke^{-r\tau}\Phi(d_2), \qquad d_{1,2} = \frac{\log(S_t/K) + (r - q \pm \tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt\tau},\] i.e. Black–Scholes with \(S_t\) replaced by \(S_te^{-q\tau}\). Special cases: a currency (\(q = r_f\), the Garman–Kohlhagen formula of Chapter 10) and a futures price (\(q = r\), Black’s formula \(e^{-r\tau}[F\Phi(d_1) - K\Phi(d_2)]\), used for interest-rate options in Chapter 8). With discrete dividends of known present value \(D\), a standard approximation replaces \(S_t\) by \(S_t - D\).
Other path-independent claims. For a payoff \(\Phi(S_T)\) the price is \(e^{-r\tau}\mathbb E^Q[\Phi(S_T)]\) with \(\log S_T \sim \mathcal N(\log S_t + (r - \sigma^2/2)\tau, \sigma^2\tau)\). Useful building blocks:

title: 5  The Black–Scholes–Merton model
text:
5.7 Numerical methods
For standard payoffs the price is explicit; more complex products, or standard products in more complex models, need numerical methods:

Numerical integration. If the risk-neutral law of \(S_T\) is known — in BSM, \(\log S_T\mid S_t \sim \mathcal N\bigl(\log S_t + (r - \tfrac{\sigma^2}2)(T - t), \sigma^2(T - t)\bigr)\) — then \(\Pi_t(G) = e^{-r(T-t)}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}G(e^x)\varphi(x)\,dx\) with \(\varphi\) that Gaussian density, a one-dimensional integral. The law is explicit only in some models.
Trees. Approximate the SDE by a binomial tree (Chapter 3); hard with several stochastic factors.
PDE methods. Finite-difference schemes for the pricing PDE; complexity grows quickly with the number of factors (machine-learning methods are promising here).
Monte Carlo. Simulate many paths of the underlying under \(Q\) and average discounted payoffs; universal and simple, requires no knowledge of the law of \(S_T\) (Chapter 6).

title: 5  The Black–Scholes–Merton model
text:
5.8 Historical and implied volatility
The volatility \(\sigma\) is the crucial — and unobservable — parameter.
Historical volatility estimates \(\sigma\) from a time series of log-returns \(Z_i = \log(S_{t_i}/S_{t_{i-1}})\) with \(t_i - t_{i-1} = \Delta\): \[\hat\sigma = \frac{1}{\sqrt\Delta}\Bigl(\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Z_i - \bar Z)^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.\]
Implied volatility is calibrated from option prices: if a call trades at \(\Pi^{\mathrm{Call}}_{\mathrm{mkt}}(K, T)\), its implied volatility \(\sigma_{\mathrm{imp}}\) solves \[\Pi^{\mathrm{Call}}_{\mathrm{mkt}}(K, T) = \Pi^{\mathrm{Call}}_{BS}(K, T; \sigma_{\mathrm{imp}}).\] Since the BS price is strictly increasing in \(\sigma\), the solution is unique (found by Newton’s method or bisection). In the BSM model \(\sigma_{\mathrm{imp}}\) would be the same for all strikes and maturities. In reality it is not: the implied-volatility surface \((K, T) \mapsto \sigma_{\mathrm{imp}}(K, T)\) shows a skew (higher implied volatility for low strikes, especially on equity indices such as the SPX) and a term structure. As the saying goes, implied volatility is “the wrong number to put in the wrong formula to get the right price”. Chapter 7 develops models that fit the surface.

title: 5  The Black–Scholes–Merton model
text:
5.10 Hedging in practice
In theory, holding \(\Delta_t\) shares and rebalancing continuously replicates the derivative perfectly: \[dV_t = (V_t - \Delta_tS_t)\,r\,dt + \Delta_t\,dS_t = dF(t, S_t).\] In practice continuous rebalancing is impossible (transaction costs); the portfolio is rebalanced at discrete dates, every \(\Delta\) units of time (say, daily). Over one step, \[V_{t+\Delta} - V_t \approx (V_t - \Delta_tS_t)r\Delta + \Delta_t(S_{t+\Delta} - S_t),\] while by Taylor’s expansion, keeping the second-order (Itô) term, \[F(t + \Delta, S_{t+\Delta}) - F(t, S_t) \approx \Theta_t\Delta + \Delta_t(S_{t+\Delta} - S_t) + \frac{\Gamma_t}{2}(S_{t+\Delta} - S_t)^2 .\] The Delta terms cancel, and the hedging error over one step is \[\bigl(V_{t+\Delta} - F(t + \Delta, S_{t+\Delta})\bigr) - \bigl(V_t - F(t, S_t)\bigr) \approx \bigl(V_t - F(t, S_t)\bigr)r\Delta + \frac{\Gamma_t}{2}\Bigl(\sigma^2S_t^2\Delta - (S_{t+\Delta} - S_t)^2\Bigr),\] where we used \(rF - \Delta_trS_t - \Theta_t = \tfrac12\sigma^2S_t^2\Gamma_t\) (the BS PDE). The first term propagates the error already accumulated. The second compares the variance the model expects over \(\Delta\) with the realised squared move: it has approximately zero mean and vanishes as \(\Delta \to 0\) (continuous-time perfect hedging), but over finite steps it is a source of P&L, proportional to Gamma. Simulations of a Delta-hedged call show final P&Ls of a few cents with frequent rebalancing, and larger ones (tens of cents) with daily or static hedging.
To reduce the error one wants \(\Gamma = 0\) as well, which requires a second traded derivative, since the underlying has zero Gamma.

To hedge a short position in a derivative \(F\) (with \(\Delta^F\), \(\Gamma^F\)) using the underlying and a traded derivative \(G\) on the same underlying (with \(\Delta^G\), \(\Gamma^G\)), choose \(\pi^S\) units of the underlying and \(\pi^G\) units of \(G\) such that \[\Delta^F = \pi^S + \pi^G\Delta^G, \qquad \Gamma^F = \pi^G\Gamma^G .\]

The solution is found in this order: first \(\pi^G = \Gamma^F/\Gamma^G\) (Gamma neutrality uses only \(G\)), then \(\pi^S = \Delta^F - \pi^G\Delta^G\). Making the position Delta-neutral first and then adding \(G\) would destroy Delta neutrality. In practice the procedure is applied at the level of whole portfolios of derivatives.

5.12 Exercises
Problems from Hull (H), Chapters 15 and 19, and Björk (B), Chapters 7 and 9.

(H 15.3, 15.4) Price a 3-month European put with \(S = K = 50\), \(r = 10\%\), \(\sigma = 30\%\). How does the price change if a dividend of \(1.50\) is expected in 2 months?


Solution. \(d_1 = \frac{(0.1 + 0.045)\times0.25}{0.3\times0.5} = 0.2417\), \(d_2 = 0.0917\); \(p = 50e^{-0.025}\Phi(-0.0917) - 50\Phi(-0.2417) = 2.38\). With the dividend, replace \(S\) by \(50 - 1.5e^{-0.1\times2/12} = 48.52\): the put rises to \(3.03\), since the dividend lowers the expected stock price.


(H 15.6) A stock follows GBM with \(\mu = 16\%\), \(\sigma = 35\%\), \(S_0 = 38\). What is the (real-world) probability that a 6-month European call with \(K = 40\) is exercised? And the put?


Solution. \(\mathbb P(S_T > K) = \Phi\bigl(\frac{\log(38/40) + (0.16 - 0.35^2/2)\times0.5}{0.35\sqrt{0.5}}\bigr) = \Phi(-0.0077) = 0.497\); the put is exercised with probability \(0.503\). These use \(\mu\); risk-neutral probabilities would use \(r\) instead.


(H 15.14) A 3-month call with \(K = 13\) on a stock at \(15\) costs \(2.50\); \(r = 5\%\). Find the implied volatility.


Solution. Solving \(C_{BS}(\sigma) = 2.50\) (e.g. by bisection, the price being increasing in \(\sigma\)) gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{imp}} \approx 39.6\%\).


(B 7.2, H 15.9) In the Black–Scholes model, find the price of the “golden logarithm”, which pays \(\log S_T\) at \(T\), and verify that it solves the Black–Scholes PDE.


Solution. \(F(t, s) = e^{-r\tau}\mathbb E^Q[\log S_T] = e^{-r\tau}\bigl(\log s + (r - \tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau\bigr)\), \(\tau = T - t\). Then \(F_t = rF - e^{-r\tau}(r - \tfrac12\sigma^2)\), \(sF_s = e^{-r\tau}\), \(s^2F_{ss} = -e^{-r\tau}\), and \(F_t + rsF_s + \tfrac12\sigma^2s^2F_{ss} - rF = e^{-r\tau}\bigl[-(r - \tfrac12\sigma^2) + r - \tfrac12\sigma^2\bigr] = 0\). ✓


(B 7.4, H 15.10) Price the claim \(S_T^\beta\) and show that its price has the form \(h(t, T)S_t^\beta\).


Solution. Under \(Q\), \(S_T^\beta = S_t^\beta\exp\bigl(\beta(r - \tfrac12\sigma^2)\tau + \beta\sigma(W^Q_T - W^Q_t)\bigr)\), so \(\mathbb E^Q[S_T^\beta\mid S_t] = S_t^\beta e^{\beta(r - \sigma^2/2)\tau + \beta^2\sigma^2\tau/2}\) and the price is \(S_t^\beta\exp\bigl((\beta - 1)(r + \tfrac12\beta\sigma^2)\tau\bigr)\). Checks: \(\beta = 1\) gives \(S_t\); \(\beta = 0\) gives the bond \(e^{-r\tau}\).


(B 7.5, H 15.20) Price a binary option paying \(K\) if \(S_T \in [\alpha, \beta]\) and nothing otherwise. In particular, what is a claim paying \(100\) if \(S_T > K\) worth?


Solution. \(Ke^{-r\tau}Q(\alpha \leq S_T \leq \beta) = Ke^{-r\tau}\bigl[\Phi(d_2(\alpha)) - \Phi(d_2(\beta))\bigr]\), where \(d_2(x) = \frac{\log(S_t/x) + (r - \sigma^2/2)\tau}{\sigma\sqrt\tau}\). The digital paying \(100\) above \(K\) is worth \(100e^{-r\tau}\Phi(d_2)\): \(\Phi(d_2)\) is the risk-neutral exercise probability.


(H 15.21) A perpetual American put with strike \(K\) is exercised when the stock first hits \(H < K\). Using that \(S^{-\gamma}\) with \(\gamma = 2r/\sigma^2\) solves the time-independent Black–Scholes equation, find its value for \(S > H\), the optimal \(H\), and the option value.


Solution. For a perpetual claim \(F = F(S)\), the PDE is \(rSF' + \tfrac12\sigma^2S^2F'' - rF = 0\), with solutions \(S\) and \(S^{-\gamma}\). A bounded solution equal to \(K - H\) at \(S = H\) is \(V(S) = (K - H)(S/H)^{-\gamma}\). Maximising over \(H\), \(\frac{d}{dH}\bigl[(K - H)H^\gamma\bigr] = 0\) gives \(H^* = \frac{\gamma K}{1 + \gamma}\). Hence \(V(S) = \frac{K}{1 + \gamma}\bigl(\frac{S}{H^*}\bigr)^{-\gamma}\) for \(S > H^*\), and \(V = K - S\) below.


(H 19.2) Compute the Delta of an at-the-money 6-month European call when \(r = 10\%\) and \(\sigma = 25\%\).


Solution. \(d_1 = \frac{(0.1 + 0.03125)\times0.5}{0.25\sqrt{0.5}} = 0.3712\), so \(\Delta = \Phi(0.3712) = 0.645\).


(B 9.5, 9.6) A portfolio has \(\Delta_P = 2\), \(\Gamma_P = 3\). (a) Make it Delta- and Gamma-neutral with two derivatives \(F\) (\(\Delta_F = -1\), \(\Gamma_F = 2\)) and \(G\) (\(\Delta_G = 5\), \(\Gamma_G = -2\)). (b) Do the same using \(F\) and the underlying.


Solution. 

Holdings \(x\) of \(F\), \(y\) of \(G\): \(2 - x + 5y = 0\), \(3 + 2x - 2y = 0\), giving \(x = -2.375\), \(y = -0.875\) (sell both). (b) Gamma first: \(3 + 2x = 0\), \(x = -1.5\); then Delta: \(2 + 1.5 + y = 0\), \(y = -3.5\) units of the underlying.



(B 9.8, 9.9) Show that for any self-financing portfolio of derivatives on the same underlying, \(\Theta_P + rS\Delta_P + \tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma_P = rP\), and deduce that a Delta- and Gamma-neutral portfolio earns the risk-free rate.


Solution. Each derivative’s pricing function solves the Black–Scholes PDE, which is linear, so the portfolio value \(P\) solves it too: this is the identity. If \(\Delta_P = \Gamma_P = 0\), it reduces to \(\Theta_P = rP\): the value changes only deterministically, at rate \(r\) — the portfolio replicates the bank account.

title: 6  Monte Carlo methods
text:
6.1 The basic method
Risk-neutral valuation expresses every price as an expectation, \(\Pi_0(G) = e^{-rT}\mathbb E^Q[G(S_T)]\). When the payoff or the model is complicated, the expectation cannot be computed in closed form — but it can be estimated by simulation. The Monte Carlo method is simple, universal, and indifferent to the dimension of the problem; its weakness is slow convergence, of order \(1/\sqrt M\) in the number of simulations. This chapter presents the method, analyses its two sources of error, and develops the three classical variance-reduction techniques: antithetic variates, control variates and importance sampling.
In the BSM model, \(\log S_T \sim \mathcal N\bigl(\log S_0 + (r - \sigma^2/2)T, \sigma^2T\bigr)\) under \(Q\). To price \(G(S_T)\):
The justification is the law of large numbers: \(\frac1M\sum_kG(S^k_T) \to \mathbb E^Q[G(S_T)]\) almost surely as \(M \to \infty\).

title: 6  Monte Carlo methods
6  Monte Carlo methods
text:
6.2 Error analysis
The error splits into two parts: \[\Pi_0(g) - e^{-rT}\frac1M\sum_kg(\hat S^k) = \underbrace{e^{-rT}\bigl(\mathbb E^Q[g(S)] - \mathbb E^Q[g(\hat S)]\bigr)}_{\text{discretisation error (bias)}} + \underbrace{e^{-rT}\Bigl(\mathbb E^Q[g(\hat S)] - \frac1M\sum_kg(\hat S^k)\Bigr)}_{\text{statistical error}} .\]
Statistical error. By the central limit theorem, \[\frac{\sqrt M\bigl(\frac1M\sum_kg(\hat S^k) - \mathbb E^Q[g(\hat S)]\bigr)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}^Q(g(\hat S))}} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal N(0, 1),\] which gives the asymptotic confidence interval of level \(1 - \alpha\) \[\frac1M\sum_kg(\hat S^k) \pm \frac{q_{1-\alpha/2}}{\sqrt M}\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}^Q(g(\hat S))},\] with \(q_{0.975} = 1.96\) for 95%. In practice the variance is replaced by the sample variance. The error decays like \(1/\sqrt M\): one more correct digit costs 100 times more simulations.
Discretisation error (bias). \(\mathrm{Bias} = \mathbb E^Q[g(S)] - \mathbb E^Q[g(\hat S)]\). For geometric Brownian motion compare the Euler scheme \[\hat S_{t+\Delta} = \hat S_t\bigl(1 + r\Delta + \sigma\Delta W^Q_t\bigr)\] with the exact scheme \[\hat S_{t+\Delta} = \hat S_t\exp\bigl((r - \sigma^2/2)\Delta + \sigma\Delta W^Q_t\bigr).\] Already after one step, \(\mathbb E^Q[\hat S_\Delta] = S_0(1 + r\Delta) < S_0e^{r\Delta} = \mathbb E^Q[S_\Delta]\) for Euler (e.g. \(101.25\) against \(101.258\) with \(S_0 = 100\), \(r = 5\%\), \(\Delta = 0.25\)), while the exact scheme has no bias: simulating from the exact distribution, when it is known, eliminates the discretisation error.
Mean square error. Accuracy is measured by \[\mathrm{MSE} = \mathbb E\Bigl[\Bigl(\mathbb E[g(S)] - \frac1M\sum_kg(\hat S^k)\Bigr)^2\Bigr] = \mathrm{Bias}^2 + \mathrm{Var}\Bigl(\frac1M\sum_kg(\hat S^k)\Bigr),\] so a good computation balances bias (a finer time grid, \(N \uparrow\)) against sampling error (\(M \uparrow\)) for a given budget. Monte Carlo parallelises trivially.

title: 6  Monte Carlo methods
text:
6.3 Generating random numbers
Every simulation starts from pseudo-random uniform numbers \(U \sim \mathcal U(0,1)\), produced by deterministic generators (linear congruential generators, the Mersenne twister) that must have a long period and pass statistical tests. Other distributions are obtained by transformation:

Inversion. If \(F\) is a continuous distribution function, \(X = F^{-1}(U)\) has distribution \(F\), since \(\mathbb P(F^{-1}(U) \leq x) = \mathbb P(U \leq F(x)) = F(x)\). Example: \(X = -\log(U)/\lambda\) is exponential. For the normal distribution \(\Phi^{-1}\) is computed by accurate rational approximations (Moro’s algorithm).
Box–Muller. If \(U_1, U_2\) are independent uniforms, \[Z_1 = \sqrt{-2\log U_1}\cos(2\pi U_2), \qquad Z_2 = \sqrt{-2\log U_1}\sin(2\pi U_2)\] are independent \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). (In polar coordinates the squared radius of a standard 2D Gaussian is exponential with mean \(2\) and the angle is uniform.) Marsaglia’s polar method avoids the trigonometric functions by rejection sampling on the unit disc.
Correlated normals. For a covariance matrix \(\Sigma = LL^\top\) (Cholesky factorisation), \(X = LZ\) with \(Z\) standard normal has covariance \(\Sigma\). In two dimensions, \(Z_1\) and \(\rho Z_1 + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}Z_2\) — the construction of correlated Brownian motions in Chapter 7.

title: 6  Monte Carlo methods
text:
6.4 Discretisation schemes for SDEs
When the law of the solution is not explicit, the SDE \(dX_t = a(X_t)\,dt + b(X_t)\,dW_t\) is integrated numerically on a grid of step \(h = \Delta t\).

\[\text{Euler–Maruyama:}\quad \hat X_{j+1} = \hat X_j + a(\hat X_j)h + b(\hat X_j)\Delta W_j,\] \[\text{Milstein:}\quad \hat X_{j+1} = \hat X_j + a(\hat X_j)h + b(\hat X_j)\Delta W_j + \tfrac12b(\hat X_j)b'(\hat X_j)\bigl((\Delta W_j)^2 - h\bigr),\] with \(\Delta W_j \sim \mathcal N(0, h)\) independent.

The Milstein correction comes from the next term of the Itô–Taylor expansion, the double integral \(\int\!\!\int dW\,dW = \tfrac12((\Delta W)^2 - h)\). For GBM (\(b(x) = \sigma x\)) it reads \(\hat X_{j+1} = \hat X_j\bigl(1 + rh + \sigma\Delta W_j + \tfrac12\sigma^2((\Delta W_j)^2 - h)\bigr)\).

A scheme converges strongly with order \(\gamma\) if \(\mathbb E|X_T - \hat X_T| = O(h^\gamma)\) (pathwise accuracy), and weakly with order \(\beta\) if \(|\mathbb E[g(X_T)] - \mathbb E[g(\hat X_T)]| = O(h^\beta)\) for smooth \(g\) (accuracy of expectations).

Euler has strong order \(\tfrac12\) and weak order \(1\); Milstein has strong order \(1\) (weak order still \(1\)). For pricing, only weak convergence matters, so Euler is often enough; strong convergence matters for path-dependent quantities and for multilevel Monte Carlo. Minimising the MSE for a fixed budget \(C\) gives \(\mathrm{MSE} = O\bigl(C^{-2\beta/(1 + 2\beta)}\bigr)\): for Euler (\(\beta = 1\)), \(O(C^{-2/3})\), slower than the \(O(C^{-1})\) of exact simulation.

title: 6  Monte Carlo methods
text:
6.5 Variance reduction
Rather than increasing \(M\), reduce the variance of what is being averaged. The three standard techniques exploit increasing amounts of problem-specific information. All the numbers below are for \(S_0 = 100\), \(r = 5\%\), \(\sigma = 20\%\), \(T = 1\) and \(M = 10^4\) (95% half-widths).

6.5.1 Antithetic variates
If \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\), then \(-Z\) has the same law: the sample \(\{-Z^k\}\) is as good as \(\{Z^k\}\), and large values in one are paired with small values in the other, so errors tend to cancel.

Two identically distributed random variables \(X\), \(Y\) are antithetic if \(\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) \leq 0\).


Let \(g\) be monotone. Then \(\mathrm{Cov}(g(X), g(-X)) \leq 0\) for any random variable \(X\), and \(\mathrm{Cov}(g(U), g(1 - U)) \leq 0\) for any \(U\). (The first is useful when \(X\) is symmetric about \(0\), the second for \(U \sim \mathrm{Unif}(0,1)\).)

Proof. Let \(f(x) = -g(-x)\); \(f\) and \(g\) are monotone in the same direction. With \(Y\) an independent copy of \(X\), \((g(X) - g(Y))(f(X) - f(Y)) \geq 0\). Taking expectations and using independence, \[0 \leq 2\,\mathbb E[g(X)f(X)] - 2\,\mathbb E[g(X)]\,\mathbb E[f(X)] = 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(g(X), f(X)) = -2\,\mathrm{Cov}(g(X), g(-X)). \qquad\square\]
For symmetric \(X\), the estimator \(\frac{g(X) + g(-X)}{2}\) is unbiased for \(\mathbb E[g(X)]\) and \[\mathrm{Var}\Bigl(\frac{g(X) + g(-X)}{2}\Bigr) = \frac{\mathrm{Var}(g(X))}{2}(1 + \rho), \qquad \rho = \mathrm{Corr}(g(X), g(-X)) \leq 0 .\]

Generate \(Z^k\) i.i.d. \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), set \(S^k_T = S_0e^{(r - \sigma^2/2)T + \sigma\sqrt TZ^k}\) and \(S^{-,k}_T = S_0e^{(r - \sigma^2/2)T - \sigma\sqrt TZ^k}\), and estimate \[\Pi_0(G) \approx e^{-rT}\frac1M\sum_{k=1}^M\frac{G(S^k_T) + G(S^{-,k}_T)}{2}.\] For path-dependent payoffs, each path built from increments \(Z^k_j\) is paired with the path built from \(-Z^k_j\).

The estimator is unbiased and consistent, and confidence intervals follow from the CLT applied to the pairs. Its variance is \(\frac{\mathrm{Var}(G(S_T))}{2M}(1 + \rho)\): compared with \(2M\) independent samples (the same number of payoff evaluations) it wins iff \(\rho < 0\), which is guaranteed when \(G\) is monotone.

Figure: a simulated path (black) and its antithetic path (grey), driven by the opposite Gaussian increments.


6.5.2 Control variates
Use the known error on a quantity we can compute to correct the estimate of one we cannot.

Let \(Y\) be a random variable with known mean, and for \(c \in \mathbb R\) let \(\tilde X = X + c(Y - \mathbb E[Y])\). Then \(\mathbb E[\tilde X] = \mathbb E[X]\) and \[\mathrm{Var}(\tilde X) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + c^2\mathrm{Var}(Y) + 2c\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y),\] minimised by \(c^* = -\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)/\mathrm{Var}(Y)\), which gives \(\mathrm{Var}(\tilde X) = \mathrm{Var}(X)\bigl(1 - \rho_{XY}^2\bigr)\).

The stronger the correlation between \(X\) and the control \(Y\), the larger the reduction; any \(c\) with \(c^2\mathrm{Var}(Y) + 2c\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y) < 0\) still helps. Intuition (for \(\rho > 0\)): if the simulated control came out above its known mean, the target was probably overestimated too, and is corrected downwards.

To price \(G(S_T)\) using a payoff \(H(S_T)\) whose price is known, \[\Pi_0(G) \approx e^{-rT}\frac1M\sum_{k=1}^M\Bigl[G(S^k_T) + c\bigl(H(S^k_T) - \mathbb E^Q[H(S_T)]\bigr)\Bigr].\]

The cost is that of plain Monte Carlo. Since \(c^*\) is unknown, one uses the regression estimate \[\hat c = -\frac{\sum_k(G(S^k_T) - \bar G)(H(S^k_T) - \bar H)}{\sum_k(H(S^k_T) - \bar H)^2},\] at the price of a small bias. Choice of control: the underlying itself is universal (\(\mathbb E^Q[S_T] = S_0e^{rT}\)); for exotic payoffs, a tractable relative — for arithmetic Asian options, the geometric Asian option, whose price is explicit because the geometric average of log-normals is log-normal.


6.5.3 Importance sampling
Put more probability on the outcomes that matter.
Let \(Z > 0\) with \(\mathbb E[Z] = 1\) and define the probability \(\tilde{\mathbb P}\) by \(d\tilde{\mathbb P} = Z\,d\mathbb P\). Then \[\mathbb E[X] = \tilde{\mathbb E}\Bigl[\frac XZ\Bigr], \qquad \mathrm{Var}_{\tilde{\mathbb P}}\Bigl(\frac XZ\Bigr) = \mathbb E\Bigl[\frac{X^2}{Z}\Bigr] - \mathbb E[X]^2,\] which can be much smaller than \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mathbb E[X^2] - \mathbb E[X]^2\). Any \(Y > 0\) with finite mean gives a valid \(Z = Y/\mathbb E[Y]\). For \(X > 0\), the choice \(Z = X/\mathbb E[X]\) gives zero variance — useless, since it needs the answer — but it shows that \(Z\) should be roughly proportional to \(X\).
In the BSM model a convenient family is \[Z(\nu) = \exp\Bigl(-\nu W^Q_T - \frac{\nu^2}{2}T\Bigr), \qquad \nu \in \mathbb R,\] which is positive with \(\mathbb E^Q[Z(\nu)] = 1\).

The probability \(d\tilde Q_\nu = Z(\nu)\,dQ\) is equivalent to \(Q\), and \(\tilde W^\nu_t = W^Q_t + \nu t\) is a \(\tilde Q_\nu\)-Brownian motion.

Proof. \(\tilde Q_\nu(\Omega) = \mathbb E^Q[Z(\nu)] = 1\), and equivalence holds because \(Z(\nu) > 0\). For \(s \leq t\), \(u \in \mathbb R\) and \(A \in \mathcal F_s\), using the \(Q\)-martingale property of \(e^{-\nu W_t - \nu^2t/2}\) and the independence of increments, \[\mathbb E^{\tilde Q_\nu}\bigl[e^{u(\tilde W^\nu_t - \tilde W^\nu_s)}\mathbf 1_A\bigr] = \mathbb E^Q\Bigl[e^{(u - \nu)(W_t - W_s)}\Bigr]\,e^{-\frac{\nu^2}{2}(t-s) + u\nu(t-s)}\,\mathbb E^Q\bigl[e^{-\nu W_s - \frac{\nu^2}{2}s}\mathbf 1_A\bigr] = e^{\frac{u^2}{2}(t-s)}\,\tilde Q_\nu(A).\] So under \(\tilde Q_\nu\) the increment \(\tilde W^\nu_t - \tilde W^\nu_s\) is \(\mathcal N(0, t - s)\) and independent of \(\mathcal F_s\). \(\square\)
Under \(\tilde Q_\nu\), since \(dW^Q_t = d\tilde W^\nu_t - \nu\,dt\), \[dS_t = (r - \sigma\nu)S_t\,dt + \sigma S_t\,d\tilde W^\nu_t :\] choosing \(\nu\) shifts the drift and makes high (or low) values of \(S\) more likely. (The course slides write the new drift as \(r - \nu\); with the density \(Z(\nu)\) above it is \(r - \sigma\nu\).)

Choose \(\nu\); generate \(Z^k\) i.i.d. \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) and set \[S^k_T = S_0\exp\bigl((r - \sigma\nu - \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2})T + \sigma\sqrt TZ^k\bigr), \qquad Z^k(\nu) = \exp\bigl(-\nu\sqrt TZ^k + \tfrac{\nu^2}{2}T\bigr),\] and estimate \(\Pi_0(G) \approx e^{-rT}\frac1M\sum_kG(S^k_T)/Z^k(\nu)\).

(\(Z^k(\nu)\) is \(Z(\nu)\) evaluated on the simulated path, using \(W^Q_T = \tilde W^\nu_T - \nu T\).) The estimator is unbiased and consistent, with variance \[\frac1M\Bigl(\mathbb E^Q\Bigl[\frac{G(S_T)^2}{Z(\nu)}\Bigr] - \mathbb E^Q[G(S_T)]^2\Bigr),\] so \(\nu\) must make \(\mathbb E^Q[G^2/Z(\nu)] < \mathbb E^Q[G^2]\). For a deep out-of-the-money call (\(K \gg S_0\)) almost all plain samples pay zero; choosing \(\nu < 0\) such that \(\mathbb E^{\tilde Q_\nu}[S_T] = K\), i.e. \(\nu = \frac{1}{\sigma}\bigl(r - \frac1T\log\frac{K}{S_0}\bigr)\), centres the simulation on the exercise region. Importance sampling is the tool for rare events: deep out-of-the-money options, credit losses, ruin probabilities in insurance.

title: 6  Monte Carlo methods
text:
6.6 Exercises
Problems from Seydel (S), Tools for Computational Finance, Chapters 2–3, and Glasserman (G), Chapter 4.

(S 2, Box–Muller) Show that if \(U_1, U_2\) are independent uniforms on \((0,1)\), then \(Z_1 = \sqrt{-2\log U_1}\cos(2\pi U_2)\) and \(Z_2 = \sqrt{-2\log U_1}\sin(2\pi U_2)\) are independent standard normals.


Solution. Set \(R^2 = -2\log U_1\) and \(\Theta = 2\pi U_2\). Then \(R^2\) is exponential with mean \(2\) (density \(\tfrac12e^{-\rho/2}\)) and \(\Theta\) is uniform on \([0, 2\pi)\), independent. The joint density of \((Z_1, Z_2) = (R\cos\Theta, R\sin\Theta)\) is obtained with \(dz_1\,dz_2 = \tfrac12\,d\rho\,d\theta\) (with \(\rho = r^2\)): \(\frac{1}{2\pi}\cdot\frac12e^{-\rho/2}\cdot2 = \frac{1}{2\pi}e^{-(z_1^2 + z_2^2)/2}\), the product of two standard normal densities.


(S 3.13) Implement Monte Carlo for European options in the Black–Scholes model and test it on: (a) a vanilla put with \(S_0 = 5\), \(K = 10\), \(r = 0.06\), \(\sigma = 0.3\), \(T = 1\); (b) an up-and-out call with \(S_0 = 5\), \(K = 6\), \(r = 0.05\), \(\sigma = 0.3\), \(T = 1\) and barrier \(B = 8\). Reference values: \(4.43046\) and \(0.0983\).


Solution. 

The exact Black–Scholes put value is \(4.43046\); plain Monte Carlo with \(10^5\) samples of \(S_T\) reproduces it within about \(\pm0.005\). (b) Simulating paths with \(1000\) monitoring dates and killing those that reach \(B\) gives \(\approx 0.102\), above the continuous-barrier value \(0.0983\): with discrete monitoring the path can cross the barrier between dates unnoticed. The bias decays only like \(\sqrt{\Delta t}\); it can be removed by the Brownian-bridge crossing probability (next exercise) or by shifting the barrier by \(e^{-0.5826\,\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}}\) (Broadie–Glasserman–Kou).



(S 3.11) For a Brownian motion, let \(X_t = W_t - \frac tTW_T\) on \([0, T]\) (the Brownian bridge from \(0\) to \(0\)). Compute \(\mathrm{Var}(X_t)\) and give a way to simulate \(W_t\) conditionally on \(W_T\).


Solution. \(\mathrm{Var}(X_t) = t - 2\frac tT t + \frac{t^2}{T^2}T = t\bigl(1 - \frac tT\bigr)\). \(X_t\) is independent of \(W_T\) (zero covariance, jointly Gaussian), so given \(W_T = w\), \(W_t = \frac tTw + \sqrt{t(1 - t/T)}\,Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0,1)\). This allows generating paths “from the end” (useful with quasi-Monte Carlo) and computing barrier-crossing probabilities between monitoring dates.


(S 3.5) Write the Milstein scheme for GBM, and show that for \(dX = a\,dt + b\,dW\) with constant \(b\) it coincides with Euler.


Solution. For GBM, \(b(x) = \sigma x\), \(b' = \sigma\): \(\hat X_{j+1} = \hat X_j\bigl(1 + \mu h + \sigma\Delta W_j + \tfrac12\sigma^2((\Delta W_j)^2 - h)\bigr)\). If \(b\) is constant, \(b' = 0\) and the correction vanishes: Euler already has strong order \(1\) for additive noise.


(Weak error of Euler) For GBM with drift \(\mu\), compute \(\mathbb E[\hat X_T]\) under the Euler scheme with \(N\) steps and compare with \(\mathbb E[X_T] = X_0e^{\mu T}\).


Solution. Each step multiplies the mean by \(1 + \mu h\), so \(\mathbb E[\hat X_T] = X_0(1 + \mu T/N)^N\). Since \((1 + x/N)^N = e^x(1 - x^2/(2N) + O(N^{-2}))\), the error is \(X_0e^{\mu T}\mu^2T^2/(2N) = O(h)\): weak order one. With \(\mu = 6\%\), \(T = 1\), \(N = 16\): \(1.06172\) against \(1.06184\).


(S 3.14) Assume \(\mathrm{MSE}(h, N) = \alpha_1^2h^{2\beta} + \alpha_2^2/N\) and cost \(C = \alpha_3N/h\). Minimise the MSE for a given budget \(C\).


Solution. Substituting \(N = Ch/\alpha_3\): \(\mathrm{MSE}(h) = \alpha_1^2h^{2\beta} + \frac{\alpha_2^2\alpha_3}{Ch}\). Setting the derivative to zero gives \(h^{2\beta+1} = \frac{\alpha_2^2\alpha_3}{2\beta\alpha_1^2C}\), so \(h^* \propto C^{-1/(1+2\beta)}\) and \(\mathrm{MSE}^* \propto C^{-2\beta/(1+2\beta)}\), i.e. \(\sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}} \propto C^{-\beta/(1+2\beta)}\): \(C^{-1/3}\) for Euler, against \(C^{-1/2}\) for unbiased simulation.


(S 3.15) For the control variate \(V_\alpha = \hat V + \alpha(\hat V^* - \mathbb E\hat V^*)\), find the optimal \(\alpha\) and the optimal variance ratio \(q_0 = \mathrm{Var}(V_{\alpha_0})/\mathrm{Var}(\hat V)\) as a function of the correlation \(\rho\). Evaluate for \(\rho = 0.95\) and \(\rho = 0.8\).


Solution. \(\alpha_0 = -\mathrm{Cov}(\hat V, \hat V^*)/\mathrm{Var}(\hat V^*)\) and \(q_0 = 1 - \rho^2\): \(0.0975\) for \(\rho = 0.95\) (a tenfold reduction, worth ten times more samples) and \(0.36\) for \(\rho = 0.8\). The gain is very sensitive to \(\rho\) near \(1\).


(G 4) Derive the closed-form price of the discretely monitored geometric Asian call with payoff \(\bigl((\prod_{j=1}^NS_{t_j})^{1/N} - K\bigr)^+\), \(t_j = jT/N\), in the Black–Scholes model.


Solution. \(\frac1N\sum_j\log S_{t_j}\) is Gaussian with mean \(m = \log S_0 + (r - \sigma^2/2)\Delta\frac{N+1}{2}\) and variance \(v = \sigma^2\Delta\frac{(N+1)(2N+1)}{6N}\), with \(\Delta = T/N\) (using \(\mathrm{Var}(\sum_jW_{t_j}) = \Delta\sum_{i,j}\min(i,j) = \Delta\frac{N(N+1)(2N+1)}{6}\)). For a log-normal \(e^Y\), \(Y \sim \mathcal N(m, v)\): \(\mathbb E[(e^Y - K)^+] = e^{m + v/2}\Phi(d_1) - K\Phi(d_1 - \sqrt v)\) with \(d_1 = (m - \log K + v)/\sqrt v\); multiply by \(e^{-rT}\). With the parameters of the comparison table this gives \(5.940\).

title: 7  Volatility modelling
text:
7.1 Reading the smile
The Black–Scholes model assumes constant volatility and Gaussian log-returns, but market option prices imply a volatility surface that is far from flat, and returns are skewed and fat-tailed. This chapter introduces the two main families of models that address these shortcomings. Local volatility models make volatility a deterministic function of time and price, and can reproduce all quoted option prices exactly (Dupire’s formula). Stochastic volatility models add a second random factor, giving realistic volatility dynamics at the cost of market incompleteness; Heston’s model is the reference example. Local-stochastic volatility models combine the two, and volatility derivatives trade volatility itself.
Before modelling the smile it helps to understand what it encodes (Hull, Chapter 20).
Calls and puts share the same implied volatility. Put–call parity \(C - P = S_0 - Ke^{-rT}\) holds for market prices (by no arbitrage) and for Black–Scholes prices (as a model identity). Subtracting, \(C_{\mathrm{mkt}} - C_{BS} = P_{\mathrm{mkt}} - P_{BS}\) for any volatility: the volatility that matches the call also matches the put. The smile is therefore a property of the strike and maturity, not of the option type.
Smiles are statements about the risk-neutral distribution. By Breeden–Litzenberger (below), call prices across strikes determine \(f^Q(T, \cdot)\). Compared with the log-normal:
Smile dynamics. How the smile moves when the spot moves matters for hedging. Under sticky strike the implied volatility of a given strike is unchanged; under sticky delta (or sticky moneyness) the smile moves with the spot. Local volatility models imply smile dynamics that contradict both in the wrong direction; stochastic volatility models give more realistic behaviour.

title: 7  Volatility modelling
7  Volatility modelling
text:
7.2 Local volatility
Under the risk-neutral probability \(Q\), postulate \[dS_t = rS_t\,dt + \sigma(t, S_t)\,S_t\,dW^Q_t, \qquad S_0 = s,\] with a local volatility function \(\sigma : [0, T]\times\mathbb R_+ \to \mathbb R_+\). Volatility now varies with time and price, but no new source of randomness is introduced: the market is still complete, and the hedging argument of Chapter 5 goes through unchanged.

The pricing function \(F\) of a European payoff \(G(S_T)\) solves \[F_t + rxF_x + \frac12\sigma(t, x)^2x^2F_{xx} - rF = 0, \qquad F(T, x) = G(x),\] which in general must be solved numerically.

How should \(\sigma(t, x)\) be chosen? So that the model reproduces the call prices observed on the market for all strikes and maturities. The answer rests on a link between call prices and the risk-neutral distribution.

7.2.1 Breeden–Litzenberger
Recall the Dirac delta \(\delta\), a generalised function used under integrals: \(\int f(x)\delta(x - a)\,dx = f(a)\). Intuitively \(\delta(x - a)\) is the derivative of \(\mathbf 1_{[a, \infty)}(x)\).

Let \(C(T, K)\) be the time-0 price of a call with maturity \(T\) and strike \(K\), and \(f^Q(T, \cdot)\) the risk-neutral density of \(S_T\). Then \[\frac{\partial C}{\partial K}(T, K) = -e^{-rT}Q(S_T > K), \qquad \frac{\partial^2C}{\partial K^2}(T, K) = e^{-rT}f^Q(T, K) = e^{-rT}\mathbb E^Q[\delta(S_T - K)].\]

Proof. Writing \((x - K)^+ = \int_K^x dy\) for \(x > K\) and exchanging the order of integration, \[C(T, K) = e^{-rT}\int_K^\infty(x - K)f^Q(T, x)\,dx = e^{-rT}\int_K^\infty\Bigl(\int_y^\infty f^Q(T, x)\,dx\Bigr)dy .\] Differentiating in \(K\) gives \(-e^{-rT}\int_K^\infty f^Q(T, x)\,dx = -e^{-rT}Q(S_T > K)\), and again \(e^{-rT}f^Q(T, K)\). Finally \(f^Q(T, K) = \int f^Q(T, x)\delta(x - K)\,dx = \mathbb E^Q[\delta(S_T - K)]\). \(\square\)
Message: the risk-neutral distribution of \(S_T\) is encoded in call prices for all strikes at maturity \(T\) — equivalently, in the implied volatility smile at \(T\). Can we find \(\sigma(t, x)\) such that the model generates exactly these distributions? Yes.


7.2.2 Dupire’s formula

If call prices \(C(T, K)\) are known for all \(T, K > 0\), the local volatility function that reproduces them is uniquely given by \[\sigma^2(T, K) = \frac{\dfrac{\partial C}{\partial T}(T, K) + rK\dfrac{\partial C}{\partial K}(T, K)}{\dfrac12K^2\dfrac{\partial^2C}{\partial K^2}(T, K)} .\]

(This does not say that the local volatility model is the only model reproducing all call prices: stochastic volatility models can do so too.)
Proof. We would like to apply Itô’s formula to \((S_t - K)^+\), which is not \(C^2\). For convex functions there is the Itô–Tanaka–Meyer formula: if \(dX_t = \alpha\,dt + \beta\,dW_t\) and \(F\) is convex, \[dF(X_t) = F'(X_t)\alpha\,dt + \frac12\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dL^x_t\,F''(dx) + F'(X_t)\beta\,dW_t,\] where \(F''(dx)\) is the second derivative in the sense of distributions and \(L^x_t\) is the local time of \(X\) at level \(x\) — roughly, the time \(X\) spends near \(x\) up to \(t\) — characterised by the occupation-time formula \(\int g(x)L^x_t\,dx = \int_0^tg(X_s)\beta^2(s, X_s)\,ds\).
For \(F(x) = (x - K)^+\), \(F'(x) = \mathbf 1_{(K, \infty)}(x)\) and \(F''(dx) = \delta(x - K)\,dx\), so \(\int dL^x_t\,\delta(x - K) = \delta(S_t - K)S_t^2\sigma^2(t, S_t)\,dt\) and \[d(S_t - K)^+ = \mathbf 1_{\{S_t > K\}}rS_t\,dt + \frac12\delta(S_t - K)S_t^2\sigma^2(t, S_t)\,dt + \mathbf 1_{\{S_t > K\}}\sigma(t, S_t)S_t\,dW^Q_t .\] Discounting, \(d\bigl(e^{-rt}(S_t - K)^+\bigr) = e^{-rt}\bigl[rK\mathbf 1_{\{S_t > K\}} + \frac12\delta(S_t - K)S_t^2\sigma^2(t, S_t)\bigr]dt + (\text{martingale})\), since \(-r(S_t - K)^+ + r S_t\mathbf 1_{\{S_t > K\}} = rK\mathbf 1_{\{S_t > K\}}\). Integrating over \([0, T]\) and taking \(Q\)-expectations (the stochastic integral has zero mean), with Breeden–Litzenberger, \[C(T, K) = (S_0 - K)^+ + \int_0^T\Bigl[rKe^{-rt}Q(S_t > K) + \frac12\frac{\partial^2C}{\partial K^2}(t, K)K^2\sigma^2(t, K)\Bigr]dt .\] Differentiating in \(T\) and using \(e^{-rT}Q(S_T > K) = -\partial_KC\), \[\frac{\partial C}{\partial T} = -rK\frac{\partial C}{\partial K} + \frac12K^2\sigma^2(T, K)\frac{\partial^2C}{\partial K^2},\] which is Dupire’s formula. \(\square\)
The last equation is the Dupire forward PDE: a PDE in \((T, K)\) satisfied by call prices as functions of strike and maturity. Dupire’s formula can also be rewritten in terms of implied volatilities.
In practice only finitely many calls are quoted. One first calibrates, for each maturity, a smooth parametric function of the strike to the quoted prices or implied volatilities, then applies Dupire’s formula to it. Limitations: the result is very sensitive to the interpolation; the second derivative \(\partial^2C/\partial K^2\) in the denominator causes numerical instability; and local volatility models predict unrealistic dynamics of the smile (the smile “moves the wrong way” when the spot moves), so they are inadequate for managing volatility risk.

text:
7.3 Interlude: multi-dimensional Itô formula

\(W = (W^1, \dots, W^d)\) is a \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motion if each \(W^j\) is a Brownian motion and the components are independent. From a two-dimensional \(W\), the process \(\hat W_t = \rho W^1_t + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}W^2_t\) is a Brownian motion with \(\mathrm{Cov}(W^1_t, \hat W_t) = \rho t\), \(\rho \in [-1, 1]\). More generally, \(RW_t\) with \(R \in \mathbb R^{d\times d}\) having unit-norm rows has correlated Brownian components.

Consider an \(\mathbb R^n\)-valued process with \(dX_t = \alpha(t, X_t)\,dt + \beta(t, X_t)\,dW_t\), \(\alpha : [0,T]\times\mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^n\), \(\beta : [0,T]\times\mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^{n\times d}\), i.e. \(dX^i_t = \alpha_i\,dt + \sum_{j=1}^d\beta_{ij}\,dW^j_t\). Components driven by common Brownian motions are correlated.

Let \(f \in C^{1,2}\) and \(B = \beta\beta^\top\). Then \[df(t, X_t) = \Bigl(f_t + \sum_{i=1}^nf_{x_i}\alpha_i + \frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^nf_{x_ix_j}B_{ij}\Bigr)dt + \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^df_{x_i}\beta_{ij}\,dW^j_t .\]

Mnemonic: \(dW^i_t\,dW^j_t = \delta_{ij}\,dt\), and for correlated Brownian motions \(dW_t\,d\hat W_t = \rho\,dt\).

title: 7  Volatility modelling
text:
7.4 Stochastic volatility
To capture the dynamics of volatility, make it random. Under the real-world probability \(\mathbb P\), \[dS_t = \mu(t, S_t)S_t\,dt + \sigma_tS_t\,dW_t, \qquad d\sigma_t = a(t, \sigma_t)\,dt + b(t, \sigma_t)\,d\hat W_t,\] with \(W\), \(\hat W\) Brownian motions with correlation \(\rho\). Features:

a second random factor; \(S\) alone is no longer Markov, but the pair \((S, \sigma)\) is;
usually \(\rho < 0\), reproducing the leverage effect: volatility rises when prices fall;
these models are continuous-time limits of GARCH models; \(a\) and \(b\) may also depend on \(S\).


7.4.1 Hedging and the pricing PDE
With two sources of randomness and only one risky asset, perfect hedging is impossible: the market is incomplete. Add a second traded instrument, an arbitrary derivative with price \(H(t, S_t, \sigma_t)\), and look for the price of a payoff \(G(S_T)\) as \(F(t, S_t, \sigma_t)\). A self-financing portfolio \(\theta = (\theta^B, \theta^S, \theta^H)\) has \(dV_t = \theta^B_t\,dB_t + \theta^S_t\,dS_t + \theta^H_t\,dH_t\), and by the two-dimensional Itô formula (subscripts \(x\) for \(S\), \(v\) for \(\sigma\); arguments omitted) \[dH = \Bigl(H_t + \tfrac12H_{xx}S^2\sigma^2 + \tfrac12H_{vv}b^2 + \rho H_{xv}S\sigma b\Bigr)dt + H_x\,dS_t + H_v\,d\sigma_t,\] and the same for \(F\). Matching \(dV = dF\): the \(d\sigma_t\) terms give \(\theta^H = F_v/H_v\); the \(dS_t\) terms give \(\theta^S = F_x - \frac{F_v}{H_v}H_x\); the \(dt\) terms fix \(\theta^B\). Imposing \(V_t = F\) and rearranging yields \[\frac{F_t + rSF_x + \tfrac12S^2\sigma^2F_{xx} + \tfrac12b^2F_{vv} + \rho S\sigma bF_{xv} - rF}{F_v} = \frac{H_t + rSH_x + \tfrac12S^2\sigma^2H_{xx} + \tfrac12b^2H_{vv} + \rho S\sigma bH_{xv} - rH}{H_v}.\] Since \(F\) and \(H\) are arbitrary derivatives, both sides must equal a common function \(q(t, S_t, \sigma_t)\).

\[F_t + rxF_x + \frac12x^2v^2F_{xx} + \frac12b^2F_{vv} + \rho xvbF_{xv} - rF = qF_v, \qquad F(T, x, v) = G(x).\] Writing \(q = \varphi b - a\), \[F_t + rxF_x + aF_v + \frac12x^2v^2F_{xx} + \frac12b^2F_{vv} + \rho xvbF_{xv} - rF = \varphi bF_v,\] where \(\varphi(t, S_t, \sigma_t)\) is the market price of volatility risk.

Who determines \(\varphi\)? The market. To see its meaning, Delta-hedge a short derivative with the underlying only: \(\Pi_t = F_xS_t - F\). Using the PDE, \[d\Pi_t = r\Pi_t\,dt - F_v\,b\bigl(\varphi\,dt + d\hat W_t\bigr).\] Delta hedging leaves volatility risk, and \(\varphi\) is the extra expected return that compensates for bearing it: a volatility risk premium. By Girsanov’s theorem there is a probability \(Q \sim \mathbb P\) absorbing both the stock’s risk premium (so that \(S\) earns \(r\)) and \(\varphi\) (so that the volatility drift becomes \(-q\)). Assuming \(q\) does not depend on \(S\), the PDE involves \(q\) only, so one may as well start directly under \(Q\). Unlike in BSM, \(Q\) is not unique: it depends on \(\varphi\), and in practice it is selected by calibration to option prices.

\[dS_t = rS_t\,dt + \sigma_tS_t\,dW^Q_t, \qquad d\sigma_t = a^Q(t, \sigma_t)\,dt + b(t, \sigma_t)\,d\hat W^Q_t,\] with \(a^Q = -q\) and \(W^Q\), \(\hat W^Q\) correlated \(Q\)-Brownian motions.



7.4.2 The Heston model

With \(v_t\) the instantaneous variance, \[dS_t = rS_t\,dt + \sqrt{v_t}\,S_t\,dW^Q_t, \qquad dv_t = \theta(\kappa - v_t)\,dt + \gamma\sqrt{v_t}\,d\hat W^Q_t, \qquad d\langle W^Q, \hat W^Q\rangle_t = \rho\,dt,\] where \(\theta\) is the speed of mean reversion, \(\kappa\) the long-run variance, \(\gamma\) the volatility of volatility (“vol of vol”). The variance follows a Cox–Ingersoll–Ross process (Chapter 8), positive if \(2\theta\kappa \geq \gamma^2\) (Feller condition).

The pricing PDE becomes \[F_t + rxF_x + \theta(\kappa - v)F_v + \frac12x^2vF_{xx} + \frac12\gamma^2vF_{vv} + \rho\gamma xvF_{xv} - rF = 0, \qquad F(T, x, v) = G(x).\]
Semi-explicit pricing. Heston’s key property: the characteristic function of \(\log S_T\), \[f_{(t,x,v)}(u) = \mathbb E^Q\bigl[e^{iu\log S_T}\bigm|\log S_t = x, v_t = v\bigr],\] is explicit. The process \(t \mapsto f_{(t, \log S_t, v_t)}(u)\) is a \(Q\)-martingale, so applying Itô’s formula its \(dt\) part must vanish, which gives a PDE for \(f\); trying the affine form \[f_{(t,x,v)}(u) = \exp\bigl(A(T - t) + B(T - t)v + iux\bigr)\] reduces it to Riccati ODEs for \(A\) and \(B\), which can be solved in closed form. Call prices then follow by Fourier inversion. This tractability explains the model’s popularity.

With \(S_0 = K = 100\), \(r = 3\%\), \(T = 1\), \(v_0 = \kappa = 0.04\) (i.e. 20% volatility), \(\theta = 2\), \(\gamma = 0.3\) and \(\rho = -0.7\), Fourier inversion gives an at-the-money call price of \(9.24\) (a Monte Carlo simulation with full truncation of the variance, \(10^5\) paths and daily steps, gives \(9.26 \pm 0.07\)). The corresponding Black–Scholes implied volatilities decrease with the strike: the negative correlation produces a skew, as observed in equity markets.


Figure: implied volatility across strikes in the Heston example (bold) against the flat Black–Scholes volatility of 20% (dashed).

title: 7  Volatility modelling
text:
7.5 Local-stochastic volatility
Local volatility fits the market exactly but has unrealistic dynamics; stochastic volatility has realistic dynamics but may not fit all quotes exactly. Local-stochastic volatility (LSV) models combine them: \[dS_t = rS_t\,dt + \ell(t, S_t)\,\sigma_tS_t\,dW^Q_t,\] with \(\sigma_t\) from a stochastic volatility model (e.g. Heston) and a leverage function \(\ell(t, x)\) calibrated so that the model reproduces the market’s local volatilities (via Dupire’s formula). Pricing requires numerical methods (usually PDEs). LSV models are standard for exotic equity options and in foreign-exchange markets (Chapter 10).

title: 7  Volatility modelling
text:
7.6 Volatility derivatives
Since the late 1990s volatility itself has been traded.

With business days \(t_0, \dots, t_N\) in \([0, T]\), the annualised realised variance is \[V_T = \frac{252}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\Bigl(\log\frac{S_{t_i}}{S_{t_{i-1}}}\Bigr)^2 .\] A variance swap pays \(V_T - K_{\mathrm{var}}\) at \(T\); a volatility swap pays \(\sqrt{V_T} - K_\sigma\). Both have zero initial value when the strike is the fair one, \(K = \mathbb E^Q[\cdot]\).

They give pure exposure to realised volatility. In the Heston model the variance swap is easy: \(V_T\) approximates \(\frac1T\int_0^Tv_t\,dt\), and since \(\mathbb E^Q[v_t] = \kappa + (v_0 - \kappa)e^{-\theta t}\), \[K_{\mathrm{var}} = \mathbb E^Q\Bigl[\frac1T\int_0^Tv_t\,dt\Bigr] = \kappa + (v_0 - \kappa)\frac{1 - e^{-\theta T}}{\theta T}.\] For the volatility swap, Jensen’s inequality gives \(\mathbb E^Q[\sqrt{V_T}] \leq \sqrt{\mathbb E^Q[V_T]}\) (a convexity adjustment); in Heston it is semi-explicit. Model-free, a variance swap can be replicated statically by a portfolio of out-of-the-money options weighted by \(1/K^2\) plus dynamic trading in the underlying — the construction behind the VIX index.

title: 7  Volatility modelling
text:
7.7 Exercises
Problems from Hull (H), Chapter 20, Gatheral (Ga), and the course material.

(H 20.1, 20.4) What smile is observed when (a) both tails of the distribution of \(S_T\) are lighter than log-normal; (b) the right tail is heavier and the left tail lighter? Explain why a heavy left tail produces a downward-sloping smile.


Solution. 

Both wings are cheaper than log-normal: implied volatility is lower away from the money (an inverted smile, a “frown”). (b) Out-of-the-money calls (high strikes) are expensive and out-of-the-money puts cheap: implied volatility increases with the strike. With a heavy left tail, low-strike puts — and, by parity, low-strike calls — are worth more than in the log-normal model, so their implied volatility is higher: the skew slopes down.



(H 20.5, 20.3) (a) A call’s market price is \(3.00\) while Black–Scholes with \(\sigma = 30\%\) gives \(3.50\); Black–Scholes with \(30\%\) gives \(1.00\) for the put with the same strike and maturity. What should the put’s market price be? (b) A call and a put with the same strike and maturity have implied volatilities \(30\%\) and \(25\%\). What trade would you make?


Solution. 

\(C_{\mathrm{mkt}} - C_{BS} = P_{\mathrm{mkt}} - P_{BS}\), so \(P_{\mathrm{mkt}} = 1.00 - 0.50 = 0.50\). (b) The call is expensive relative to the put: by parity this is an arbitrage. Sell the call, buy the put, buy the stock, borrow the present value of the strike. The position is riskless at maturity and earns the price discrepancy. The argument uses only parity, so it works whatever the true distribution.



(H 20.13) A stock trades at \(60\); tomorrow a court ruling will move it to \(75\) (favourable) or \(50\) (unfavourable). What is the risk-neutral probability of a favourable ruling? What shape of smile do you expect for short-dated options?


Solution. Ignoring one day of interest, \(75p + 50(1 - p) = 60\) gives \(p = 0.4\). The distribution of \(S_T\) is a mixture of two log-normals centred near \(75\) and \(50\): bimodal, with little mass near \(60\). At-the-money options are then cheap relative to the wings (a “frown”): the opposite of the usual smile, typical before binary events such as earnings or elections.


(H 20.14) An exchange rate is \(0.80\) with quoted volatility \(12\%\), equal interest rates. Under the log-normal assumption, estimate the probabilities that in 3 months the rate is below \(0.70\), in \([0.70, 0.75]\), \([0.75, 0.80]\), \([0.80, 0.85]\), \([0.85, 0.90]\), above \(0.90\). Which are likely too low given the FX smile?


Solution. With \(\log S_T \sim \mathcal N(\log0.8 - \tfrac12\sigma^2T, \sigma^2T)\), \(\sigma\sqrt T = 0.06\): \(1.41\%\), \(13.38\%\), \(36.41\%\), \(33.90\%\), \(12.59\%\), \(2.31\%\). FX smiles indicate heavier tails than log-normal: the extreme buckets (\(< 0.70\) and \(> 0.90\)) are underestimated, and the central ones slightly overestimated.


(Breeden–Litzenberger in BSM) Show that \(e^{rT}\partial^2C/\partial K^2\) is the log-normal risk-neutral density of \(S_T\) when \(C\) is the Black–Scholes price.


Solution. From \(C = S_0\Phi(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)\), \(\partial_KC = -e^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)\) (the terms from \(\partial_Kd_{1,2}\) cancel since \(S_0\varphi(d_1) = Ke^{-rT}\varphi(d_2)\)), matching \(-e^{-rT}Q(S_T > K)\). Then \(\partial^2_KC = e^{-rT}\frac{\varphi(d_2)}{K\sigma\sqrt T}\), and \(\frac{\varphi(d_2)}{K\sigma\sqrt T}\) is the density of \(S_0e^{(r - \sigma^2/2)T + \sigma\sqrt TZ}\) at \(K\).


(Dupire consistency) Show that Dupire’s formula returns \(\sigma^2\) when call prices are given by the Black–Scholes formula with constant \(\sigma\).


Solution. \(\partial_TC = \frac{S_0\varphi(d_1)\sigma}{2\sqrt T} + rKe^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)\), \(rK\partial_KC = -rKe^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)\), and \(\tfrac12K^2\partial^2_KC = \frac{S_0\varphi(d_1)}{2\sigma\sqrt T}\). The ratio is \(\sigma^2\).


(Ga 11, variance swaps) In the Heston model with \(\theta = 2\), \(\kappa = 0.04\), find the fair 1-year variance-swap strike when \(v_0 = 0.09\). Why is the fair volatility-swap strike lower than \(\sqrt{K_{\mathrm{var}}}\)?


Solution. \(K_{\mathrm{var}} = 0.04 + 0.05\,\frac{1 - e^{-2}}{2} = 0.0616\), a volatility of \(24.8\%\). Since \(\sqrt\cdot\) is concave, Jensen gives \(\mathbb E[\sqrt{V_T}] \leq \sqrt{\mathbb E[V_T]}\): the difference (the convexity adjustment) grows with the vol of vol.


(Two-dimensional Itô) In the Heston model compute \(d(S_tv_t)\).


Solution. \(d(S_tv_t) = v_t\,dS_t + S_t\,dv_t + d\langle S, v\rangle_t\) with \(d\langle S, v\rangle_t = \rho\gamma v_tS_t\,dt\), so \(d(S_tv_t) = S_t\bigl(rv_t + \theta(\kappa - v_t) + \rho\gamma v_t\bigr)dt + S_tv_t^{3/2}dW^Q_t + \gamma S_t\sqrt{v_t}\,d\hat W^Q_t\).
