title: 8  Interest rate modelling
text:
8.1 Interest rates in the market
The Black–Scholes model takes the interest rate as a known constant. In reality rates move unpredictably, creating interest rate risk — and fixed-income derivatives make up about 80% of the OTC derivatives market. This chapter defines the various interest rates and how they are built from zero-coupon bond prices, prices the linear products (FRAs, floating-rate bonds, swaps) by pure no-arbitrage arguments, introduces the optional ones (caps, floors, swaptions), and then models the short rate with an SDE. Hedging arguments lead to the term-structure PDE and its Feynman–Kač solution; affine models (Vasiček, Cox–Ingersoll–Ross, Hull–White) make bond prices explicit.
Several rates coexist:
The rate applicable to a loan depends on credit risk, the risk that the borrower defaults. A truly risk-free rate does not exist, but derivative pricing needs one; overnight rates are used as proxies (Chapter 9).

title: 8  Interest rate modelling
text:
Treasury rates: the rate at which a government borrows in its own currency; traditionally “risk-free”, but not really (sovereign spreads).
Interbank rates (Euribor; formerly Libor, discontinued on 1 July 2023): the rate at which major banks lend to each other for a given tenor (1, 3, 6, 12 months); reference rates for an enormous volume of loans and derivatives.
Overnight rates: banks adjust their central-bank reserves by lending and borrowing overnight (€STR in the euro area, the Federal Funds rate in the US).
Repo rates: rates on secured borrowing (repurchase agreements), e.g. SOFR in the US.

title: 8  Interest rate modelling
8  Interest rate modelling
text:
8.3 Linear interest rate products

8.3.1 Forward rate agreements
Rates change: the 1-year Euribor fixed in one year, \(L_1(1, 2)\), may differ from today’s \(L_0(0, 1)\). A borrower paying a floating rate faces interest rate risk.

A FRA for the period \([S, T]\) with fixed rate \(K\) and notional \(N\) exchanges at \(T\) the floating rate \(L_S(S, T)\) (received, the floating leg) against \(K\) (paid, the fixed leg): \[\text{payoff at } T = N(T - S)\bigl(L_S(S, T) - K\bigr).\]


Today you arrange to borrow 10 000 € in one year, repaying in two years at the 1-year Euribor fixed in one year. A FRA on \([1, 2]\) with notional 10 000 € and rate \(K\) pays \(10\,000\,L_1(1, 2)\) against \(10\,000\,K\): the net cost of the loan is \(10\,000\,K\), fixed today.


For \(t \leq S\) (unit notional), \[\Pi^{FRA}_t = P_t(S) - \bigl(1 + (T - S)K\bigr)P_t(T) = (T - S)\bigl(L_t(S, T) - K\bigr)P_t(T).\] The FRA has zero value iff \(K = L_t(S, T)\): the forward rate plays the role of the forward price.

Proof. The payoff \((T - S)(L_S(S, T) - K) = \frac{1}{P_S(T)} - 1 - (T - S)K\) is known at \(S\), so its value at \(S\) is \(P_S(T)\) times it: \(1 - (1 + (T - S)K)P_S(T)\) — one ZCB maturing at \(S\) minus \(1 + (T - S)K\) ZCBs maturing at \(T\). By the law of one price this holds at every \(t \leq S\). \(\square\)


8.3.2 Floating-rate bonds and swaps

Figure: payment schedule. The floating rate for \([T_{k-1}, T_k]\) is fixed at \(T_{k-1}\) and paid at \(T_k\).

A floating-rate bond with dates \(0 \leq T_0 < T_1 < \dots < T_N\) pays at each \(T_k\) the coupon \(c_k = (T_k - T_{k-1})\bigl(L_{T_{k-1}}(T_{k-1}, T_k) + \alpha\bigr)\), with a fixed spread \(\alpha\) (in basis points), plus the principal \(1\) at \(T_N\).


\[\Pi_0(\alpha) = P_0(T_0) + \alpha\sum_{k=1}^N(T_k - T_{k-1})P_0(T_k).\] In particular, a floater with zero spread is worth exactly \(P_0(T_0)\): par at the fixing date.

Proof. Split each floating coupon as \((T_k - T_{k-1})\bigl(L_{T_{k-1}}(T_{k-1}, T_k) - L_0(T_{k-1}, T_k)\bigr) + (T_k - T_{k-1})L_0(T_{k-1}, T_k)\). The first part is a FRA struck at the forward rate, worth zero. The second is a known amount paid at \(T_k\), worth \(\bigl(\frac{P_0(T_{k-1})}{P_0(T_k)} - 1\bigr)P_0(T_k) = P_0(T_{k-1}) - P_0(T_k)\). Summing telescopes to \(P_0(T_0) - P_0(T_N)\). The spreads are worth \(\alpha\sum_k(T_k - T_{k-1})P_0(T_k)\), and the principal \(P_0(T_N)\). \(\square\)

An IRS with dates \(T_0 < \dots < T_N\) and fixed rate \(S\) exchanges at each \(T_k\) the net amount \((T_k - T_{k-1})\bigl(L_{T_{k-1}}(T_{k-1}, T_k) - S\bigr)\) (payer swap: receive floating, pay fixed). It is a portfolio of \(N\) FRAs with common rate \(K = S\).


The fixed rate making the swap worthless at \(t = 0\) is \[S(T_0, \dots, T_N) = \frac{P_0(T_0) - P_0(T_N)}{\sum_{k=1}^N(T_k - T_{k-1})P_0(T_k)} .\] The denominator \(A_0 = \sum_k(T_k - T_{k-1})P_0(T_k)\) is the annuity (or PVBP).

Proof. The swap’s cash flows are those of a floater with spread \(\alpha = -S\) minus the principal, worth \(\Pi_0(-S) - P_0(T_N) = P_0(T_0) - P_0(T_N) - S\,A_0\); set it to zero. \(\square\)
For example, with a flat zero curve at 3% (continuous) and annual payments over 5 years, \(S = (1 - e^{-0.15})/\sum_{k=1}^5e^{-0.03k} = 3.045\%\) — the annually compounded equivalent of 3%.

title: 8  Interest rate modelling
section: 8.4 Options on rates: caps, floors, swaptions
text:
8.4 Options on rates: caps, floors, swaptions

A caplet on \([S, T]\) with strike \(K\) pays \((T - S)\bigl(L_S(S, T) - K\bigr)^+\) at \(T\); a floorlet pays \((T - S)\bigl(K - L_S(S, T)\bigr)^+\). A cap (floor) with dates \(T_0, \dots, T_N\) is the sum of the caplets (floorlets) on \([T_{k-1}, T_k]\).

A borrower paying a floating rate who buys a cap never pays more than \(K\); a lender receiving floating who buys a floor never receives less than \(K\). A caplet is an option on a FRA, a cap a portfolio of caplets.

The caplet is worth, at time \(S\), \[\Pi^{cpl}_S = \bigl(1 + (T - S)K\bigr)\Bigl(\frac{1}{1 + (T - S)K} - P_S(T)\Bigr)^+,\] i.e. \(1 + (T - S)K\) European puts with maturity \(S\) on the ZCB maturing at \(T\), with strike \(1/(1 + (T - S)K)\). Similarly a floorlet is a portfolio of calls on a ZCB.

Proof. \((T - S)(L_S(S,T) - K)^+ = \bigl(\frac{1}{P_S(T)} - (1 + (T - S)K)\bigr)^+\) is known at \(S\); multiplying by \(P_S(T)\) gives the value at \(S\): \(\bigl(1 - (1 + (T - S)K)P_S(T)\bigr)^+\). \(\square\)

A (payer) swaption gives the right to enter at \(T_0\) into the swap with fixed rate \(S\). Its payoff at \(T_0\) is \[\bigl(S(T_0, \dots, T_N)_{T_0} - S\bigr)^+\sum_{k=1}^N(T_k - T_{k-1})P_{T_0}(T_k),\] where \(S(T_0, \dots, T_N)_{T_0}\) is the swap rate prevailing at \(T_0\): the swap is entered only if the market rate exceeds \(S\).

Equivalently a swaption is an option on a portfolio of ZCBs, i.e. on a coupon bond. Their market pricing is described below.

8.4.1 Market practice: Black’s formula
Traders quote caplets and swaptions through Black’s (1976) formula, a log-normal model for the underlying rate rather than for the short rate. For a caplet on \([T_{k-1}, T_k]\) with accrual \(\tau_k\), strike \(K\), forward rate \(F_k = L_0(T_{k-1}, T_k)\) and volatility \(\sigma_k\): \[\mathrm{Cpl}_0 = N\tau_kP_0(T_k)\bigl[F_k\Phi(d_1) - K\Phi(d_2)\bigr], \qquad d_{1,2} = \frac{\log(F_k/K) \pm \tfrac12\sigma_k^2T_{k-1}}{\sigma_k\sqrt{T_{k-1}}}.\] For a payer swaption on a swap starting at \(T_0\), with forward swap rate \(S_0 = S(T_0, \dots, T_N)\) and annuity \(A_0 = \sum_k\tau_kP_0(T_k)\): \[\mathrm{Swpt}_0 = N A_0\bigl[S_0\Phi(d_1) - K\Phi(d_2)\bigr], \qquad d_{1,2} = \frac{\log(S_0/K) \pm \tfrac12\sigma^2T_0}{\sigma\sqrt{T_0}}.\]
These are not ad hoc. Under the \(T_k\)-forward measure \(Q^{T_k}\) — the probability with numeraire \(P_t(T_k)\) instead of the bank account — the forward rate \(L_t(T_{k-1}, T_k) = \frac{1}{\tau_k}\bigl(\frac{P_t(T_{k-1})}{P_t(T_k)} - 1\bigr)\) is a ratio of a traded asset to the numeraire, hence a martingale, and \[\mathrm{Cpl}_0 = N\tau_kP_0(T_k)\,\mathbb E^{Q^{T_k}}\bigl[(L_{T_{k-1}}(T_{k-1}, T_k) - K)^+\bigr].\] If the forward rate is log-normal under \(Q^{T_k}\), this is exactly Black’s formula (the LIBOR market model makes this assumption for all forward rates simultaneously). Likewise the swap rate is a martingale under the annuity measure with numeraire \(A_t\). Caps are then quoted by a single flat volatility applied to all their caplets, or by caplet-specific spot volatilities. When rates can be negative, the Bachelier (normal) model, \(dF = \sigma_N\,dW\), replaces the log-normal one.

title: 8  Interest rate modelling
text:
8.5 Short-rate models
Model the short rate under \(\mathbb P\) by \[dr_t = \mu(t, r_t)\,dt + \sigma(t, r_t)\,dW_t .\] ZCBs are taken as the fundamental traded assets, for every maturity \(T\). Since \(r\) is Markov, look for prices of the form \(P_t(T) = F^T(t, r_t)\).

8.5.1 The term-structure PDE

Portfolio of two bonds. Fix maturities \(S < T\) and a self-financing \(\theta = (\theta^S, \theta^T)\) in the two ZCBs: \(V_t = \theta^S_tP_t(S) + \theta^T_tP_t(T)\), \(dV_t = \theta^S_t\,dP_t(S) + \theta^T_t\,dP_t(T)\), where by Itô’s formula \[dF^T(t, r_t) = \Bigl(F^T_t + \mu F^T_r + \tfrac12\sigma^2F^T_{rr}\Bigr)dt + \sigma F^T_r\,dW_t .\]
Make it riskless. Choose \(\theta^S_t = -\theta^T_tF^T_r/F^S_r\), which kills the \(dW_t\) term.
No arbitrage. A riskless portfolio must earn the short rate: \(dV_t = r_tV_t\,dt\). After simplification, \[\frac{F^T_t + \tfrac12\sigma^2F^T_{rr} - rF^T}{F^T_r} = \frac{F^S_t + \tfrac12\sigma^2F^S_{rr} - rF^S}{F^S_r}.\]
Separation. Since \(S\) and \(T\) are arbitrary, both sides equal a function \(q(t, r_t)\) independent of maturity. Writing \(q = \lambda\sigma - \mu\):


For every \(T > 0\), \[F^T_t + (\mu - \lambda\sigma)F^T_r + \frac12\sigma^2F^T_{rr} - rF^T = 0, \qquad F^T(T, r) = 1,\] where \(\lambda(t, r)\) is the market price of interest rate risk.

Why does \(\lambda\) appear? In BSM there is one source of risk and one exogenously given risky asset to hedge it; here the only exogenous asset is the bank account, and the short rate is not a traded asset. The real-world dynamics of \(r\) alone do not determine bond prices: one must also know \(\lambda\), which is set by the market — in practice, by calibration.

The solution of the term-structure PDE is \[P_t(T) = F^T(t, r_t) = \mathbb E^Q\Bigl[e^{-\int_t^Tr_u\,du}\Bigm|r_t\Bigr],\] where under \(Q\) the short rate follows \(dr_t = \bigl(\mu - \lambda\sigma\bigr)(t, r_t)\,dt + \sigma(t, r_t)\,dW^Q_t\).

Under this risk-neutral probability every ZCB has expected return \(r_t\). Prices depend on \(\mu\) and \(\lambda\) only through the risk-neutral drift \(\mu^Q = \mu - \lambda\sigma = -q\). Hence the usual practice of risk-neutral modelling: specify \(r\) directly under \(Q\) and calibrate its parameters to market prices.


8.5.2 Affine models

A model \(dr_t = \mu^Q(t, r_t)\,dt + \sigma(t, r_t)\,dW^Q_t\) is affine if \[\mu^Q(t, r) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1r, \qquad \sigma^2(t, r) = \beta_0 + \beta_1r .\]

Try the exponential-affine ansatz \(F^T(t, r) = \exp\bigl(A(T - t) - B(T - t)r\bigr)\). Substituting into the PDE (with \(\tau = T - t\), so \(\partial_t = -\partial_\tau\)), \[-A'(\tau) - \bigl(1 - B'(\tau)\bigr)r - (\alpha_0 + \alpha_1r)B(\tau) + \tfrac12(\beta_0 + \beta_1r)B(\tau)^2 = 0 .\] This must hold for all \(r\), so the constant and the coefficient of \(r\) vanish separately: \[B'(\tau) = 1 + \alpha_1B(\tau) - \tfrac12\beta_1B(\tau)^2, \qquad A'(\tau) = -\alpha_0B(\tau) + \tfrac12\beta_0B(\tau)^2, \qquad A(0) = B(0) = 0 .\] The equation for \(B\) is a Riccati ODE; \(A\) then follows by integration. The PDE has been reduced to ODEs, solvable explicitly in the classical cases.


8.5.3 Vasiček

\[dr_t = \theta(\kappa - r_t)\,dt + \gamma\,dW^Q_t,\] with speed of mean reversion \(\theta\), long-run mean \(\kappa\), volatility \(\gamma\).

This is an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process (Chapter 4): \[r_t = r_0e^{-\theta t} + \kappa(1 - e^{-\theta t}) + \gamma\int_0^te^{-\theta(t-u)}dW^Q_u,\] Gaussian with \(\mathbb E^Q[r_t] = r_0e^{-\theta t} + \kappa(1 - e^{-\theta t})\) and \(\mathrm{Var}^Q(r_t) = \frac{\gamma^2}{2\theta}(1 - e^{-2\theta t})\). The rate can become negative — once seen as a defect, but a feature after 2014. Here \(\alpha_0 = \theta\kappa\), \(\alpha_1 = -\theta\), \(\beta_0 = \gamma^2\), \(\beta_1 = 0\), and \[B(\tau) = \frac{1 - e^{-\theta\tau}}{\theta}, \qquad A(\tau) = \Bigl(\kappa - \frac{\gamma^2}{2\theta^2}\Bigr)\bigl(B(\tau) - \tau\bigr) - \frac{\gamma^2}{4\theta}B(\tau)^2 .\] (The course slides print \(\kappa - \gamma^2/2\) in the first factor; the correct factor is \(\kappa - \gamma^2/(2\theta^2)\).) Caplets and floorlets have Black–Scholes-like closed forms, since bond prices are log-normal.


8.5.4 Cox–Ingersoll–Ross

\[dr_t = \theta(\kappa - r_t)\,dt + \gamma\sqrt{r_t}\,dW^Q_t .\]

The rate stays non-negative, and strictly positive if \(2\kappa\theta \geq \gamma^2\) (Feller condition). \(r_t\) follows a non-central chi-square distribution, with the same mean as in Vasiček and variance \[\mathrm{Var}^Q(r_t) = r_0\frac{\gamma^2}{\theta}\bigl(e^{-\theta t} - e^{-2\theta t}\bigr) + \frac{\kappa\gamma^2}{2\theta}\bigl(1 - e^{-\theta t}\bigr)^2 .\] It is the same SDE as the variance in the Heston model. With \(h = \sqrt{\theta^2 + 2\gamma^2}\), \[B(\tau) = \frac{2(e^{h\tau} - 1)}{2h + (\theta + h)(e^{h\tau} - 1)}, \qquad A(\tau) = \frac{2\kappa\theta}{\gamma^2}\log\frac{2he^{(\theta + h)\tau/2}}{2h + (\theta + h)(e^{h\tau} - 1)} .\] Caplets and floorlets are semi-explicit.

With \(r_0 = 3\%\), \(\theta = 0.5\), \(\kappa = 4\%\) and \(T = 5\): Vasiček with \(\gamma = 1\%\) gives \(P_0(5) = 0.8343\) (yield \(3.62\%\)); CIR with \(\gamma = 5\%\) (Feller holds: \(0.04 > 0.0025\)) gives \(P_0(5) = 0.8342\), confirmed by a Monte Carlo simulation (\(0.8342\)). The yield lies between \(r_0\) and \(\kappa\), pulled down slightly by the convexity term \(-\gamma^2/(2\theta^2)\).



8.5.5 Hull–White: fitting today’s curve
Vasiček and CIR have three or four parameters and cannot reproduce an arbitrary observed term structure. The Hull–White model (extended Vasiček) makes the drift time-dependent: \[dr_t = \bigl(\alpha(t) - \theta r_t\bigr)dt + \gamma\,dW^Q_t,\] still Gaussian and mean-reverting, with \(\mathbb E^Q[r_t] = r_0e^{-\theta t} + \int_0^te^{-\theta(t-u)}\alpha(u)\,du\). It is affine with \(B(\tau) = (1 - e^{-\theta\tau})/\theta\) as in Vasiček and \[A(T - t) = \int_t^T\Bigl(\frac{\gamma^2}{2}B(T - u)^2 - \alpha(u)B(T - u)\Bigr)du .\] The model forward curve is \(f_0(T) = -\partial_T\log P_0(T) = -\partial_TA(T) + \partial_TB(T)\,r_0\). Requiring \(f_0(T) = f^{\mathrm{mkt}}_0(T)\) for all \(T\) determines \(\alpha\) uniquely: \[\alpha(T) = \frac{\partial}{\partial T}f^{\mathrm{mkt}}_0(T) + \theta f^{\mathrm{mkt}}_0(T) + \frac{\gamma^2}{2\theta}\bigl(1 - e^{-2\theta T}\bigr).\] The model then reproduces today’s curve exactly by construction, and \(\theta\), \(\gamma\) are calibrated to option prices (caplets, swaptions), which also have closed forms.






Short-rate models are the natural first step but have limitations: one factor implies perfectly correlated rates of all maturities. Richer approaches model the whole forward curve (Heath–Jarrow–Morton) or the market forward rates directly (LIBOR/forward market models). After 2008 the spread between interbank and overnight rates forced a multi-curve framework, and the 2023 end of Libor moved markets to backward-looking risk-free rates — the subject of Chapter 9.

title: 8  Interest rate modelling
text:
8.6 Exercises
Problems from Hull (H), Chapters 7, 29 and 31, and Björk (B), Chapters 22–23.

(B 22.1) In a FRA with continuous compounding, the lender pays \(K\) at \(S\) and receives \(Ke^{R^*(T - S)}\) at \(T\). (a) Value the contract at \(t < S\) in terms of ZCB prices. (b) Show that it is worth zero iff \(R^*\) equals the forward rate.


Solution. 

\(\Pi_t = -KP_t(S) + Ke^{R^*(T-S)}P_t(T)\). (b) \(\Pi_t = 0\) iff \(e^{R^*(T-S)} = P_t(S)/P_t(T)\), i.e. \(R^* = -\frac{\log P_t(T) - \log P_t(S)}{T - S} = F_t(S, T)\).



(H 7.2) A swap on \(100\) million has 10 months to run: six-month Libor is received against \(4\%\) (semiannual) paid. Forward Libor rates for all maturities are \(3\%\) (semiannual); the Libor fixed two months ago was \(2.4\%\); OIS rates are \(2.7\%\) (continuous) for discounting. Value the swap for both parties.


Solution. Payments in 4 and 10 months. Fixed leg: \(2\)m each. Floating: \(0.5 \times 2.4\% \times 100 = 1.2\)m (already fixed) and \(1.5\)m (at the forward rate). To the party paying floating and receiving fixed: \((2 - 1.2)e^{-0.027/3} + (2 - 1.5)e^{-0.027\times10/12} = 1.282\)m. To the party paying fixed: \(-1.282\)m.


(H 29.1) A company caps 3-month Libor at \(2\%\) on \(20\) million. At a reset date the rate is \(4\%\). What payment results, and when?


Solution. \(20\,000\,000 \times 0.25 \times (0.04 - 0.02) = 100\,000\), paid three months after the reset date (at the end of the accrual period).


(H 29.5) Price a caplet on the 3-month rate for the period from 15 to 18 months, struck at \(13\%\) (quarterly compounding), on a principal of \(1000\). The forward rate is \(12\%\), the 18-month zero rate is \(11.5\%\) (continuous), and the forward-rate volatility is \(12\%\).


Solution. Black’s formula with \(F = 0.12\), \(K = 0.13\), \(T_{k-1} = 1.25\), \(\sigma = 0.12\): \(d_1 = \frac{\log(12/13) + \frac12\,0.12^2\times1.25}{0.12\sqrt{1.25}} = -0.5295\), \(d_2 = -0.6637\), so \(F\Phi(d_1) - K\Phi(d_2) = 0.12\times0.2982 - 0.13\times0.2534 = 0.00284\). The price is \(1000 \times 0.25 \times e^{-0.115\times1.5} \times 0.00284 = 0.60\).


(H 29.14) Value a European swaption giving the right to enter in 4 years a 3-year annual-pay swap paying \(5\%\) fixed on \(10\) million. All swap rates are \(5\%\), OIS rates \(4.7\%\) (continuous), swap-rate volatility \(20\%\).


Solution. Annuity \(A = e^{-0.047\times5} + e^{-0.047\times6} + e^{-0.047\times7} = 2.2645\). At the money (\(S_0 = K = 5\%\)): \(d_{1,2} = \pm\tfrac12\times0.2\times2 = \pm0.2\), and the swaption is worth \(10^7 \times 2.2645 \times 0.05\,(\Phi(0.2) - \Phi(-0.2)) = 179\,500\).


(H 29.11, B 23.3) (a) Derive a put–call parity for swaptions. (b) Find the fixed rate \(R\) that makes a contract exchanging \(K(e^{RT} - 1)\) against \(K(e^{\int_0^Tr_s\,ds} - 1)\) at \(T\) worthless.


Solution. 

Payer minus receiver swaption with the same strike \(K\) pays \((S_{T_0} - K)^+A_{T_0} - (K - S_{T_0})^+A_{T_0} = (S_{T_0} - K)A_{T_0}\), the value of a forward-starting payer swap at rate \(K\): \(\mathrm{Payer} - \mathrm{Receiver} = A_0(S_0 - K)\). (b) The value is \(K\bigl(e^{RT}P_0(T) - \mathbb E^Q[e^{-\int_0^Tr}e^{\int_0^Tr}]\bigr) = K\bigl(e^{RT}P_0(T) - 1\bigr)\), zero iff \(R = -\log P_0(T)/T\): the \(T\)-year zero rate, whatever the short-rate model.



(H 31.4) In the risk-neutral Vasiček model with speed \(0.1\), level \(0.03\) and volatility \(0.01\), price a 5-year ZCB with principal \(1\) when \(r_0 = 2\%\).


Solution. \(B(5) = (1 - e^{-0.5})/0.1 = 3.935\), \(A(5) = (0.03 - 0.01^2/0.02)(3.935 - 5) - 0.01^2\times3.935^2/0.4 = -0.03050\), so \(P = e^{A - Br_0} = e^{-0.03050 - 0.0787} = 0.8966\).


(H 31.9) In both Vasiček and CIR take speed \(0.1\), level \(0.1\), \(r_0 = 10\%\), and an initial short-rate volatility of \(2\%\) (so \(\gamma = 0.02\) in Vasiček and \(\gamma\sqrt{0.1} = 0.02\) in CIR). Compare the 10-year ZCB prices.


Solution. Vasiček: \(0.3805\). CIR with \(\gamma = 0.0632\): \(0.3799\). The models agree closely when calibrated to the same initial volatility; they differ more for long maturities and for distributions of future rates (CIR cannot go negative; its volatility falls as rates fall).


(B 22.5) Show that \(f(0, T) = y(0, T) + T\,\partial_Ty(0, T)\), where \(y\) is the zero-coupon yield, and that for an increasing yield curve \(y_M(0, T) \leq y(0, T) \leq f(0, T)\), \(y_M\) being the yield of a coupon bond. Interpret.


Solution. \(P(0, T) = e^{-Ty(0,T)}\), so \(f = -\partial_T\log P = y + Ty'\). If \(y' \geq 0\), then \(f \geq y\). A coupon bond’s yield is a weighted average of the zero yields at its payment dates, all \(\leq T\), so \(y_M \leq y(0, T)\). The forward rate is the marginal rate at \(T\), the zero yield the average over \([0, T]\), and the coupon yield a further average — marginal above average when the curve rises.


(B 22.7) A consol pays \(1\) at \(t = 1, 2, \dots\) forever, with a flat continuously compounded yield \(y\). Compute its price, duration and convexity.


Solution. With \(x = e^{-y}\): price \(P = \sum_{n\geq1}x^n = \frac{x}{1 - x} = \frac{1}{e^y - 1}\). Duration \(D = \frac1P\sum nx^n = \frac{1}{1 - x} = \frac{e^y}{e^y - 1}\) (also \(-P'(y)/P\)). Convexity \(\frac1P\sum n^2x^n = \frac{1 + x}{(1 - x)^2}\). For \(y = 5\%\): \(P = 19.50\), \(D = 20.50\) years, \(C = 820\).


(Vasiček bond price, directly) Show that \(\int_t^Tr_u\,du\) is Gaussian in the Vasiček model and recover \(P_t(T) = e^{A(\tau) - B(\tau)r_t}\) from \(\mathbb E^Q[e^{-\int_t^Tr_u\,du}\mid r_t]\).


Solution. It is a linear functional of a Gaussian process, with mean \(m = \kappa\tau + (r_t - \kappa)B(\tau)\) and variance \(v = \frac{\gamma^2}{\theta^2}\bigl(\tau - 2B(\tau) + \frac{1 - e^{-2\theta\tau}}{2\theta}\bigr)\), \(\tau = T - t\). Then \(\mathbb E[e^{-X}] = e^{-m + v/2}\), which simplifies to \(e^{A(\tau) - B(\tau)r_t}\).

title: 9  Risk-free rates in practice
text:
9.1 The fixed-income market
Chapter 8 treated the risk-free curve as a given mathematical object. In practice it has to be built from market quotes, under precise conventions, and since 2023 from a new family of benchmarks. This chapter, based on a practitioner lecture by Vincenzo Russo (Assicurazioni Generali), covers market conventions, the transition from interbank offered rates (IBORs) to overnight risk-free rates (RFRs), the pricing of overnight indexed swaps, swaptions and caplets on backward-looking rates, the bootstrap of an RFR curve, and the use of risk-free curves in the insurance sector under Solvency II.
The fixed-income market trades debt securities that pay predetermined cash flows: government bonds, corporate and covered bonds, municipal bonds, securitised products (MBS, ABS), money-market instruments. Issuers are sovereigns and financial or non-financial corporates; investors (asset managers, insurers, banks, pension funds) seek income, capital preservation, diversification and liability matching. Bonds differ by maturity (money market below 1 year, short 1–3, intermediate 3–7, long beyond 7), currency, structure (fixed, floating, inflation-linked, callable or putable, securitised) and credit rating (AAA down to D).
Prices and yields move inversely. The total yield of a risky bond decomposes as \[\text{yield} = \text{risk-free rate} + \text{credit spread} + \text{liquidity premium},\] so the risk-free curve is the reference for everything: discounting cash flows (time value of money without credit risk), forwarding floating rates (forward rates implied by no arbitrage), risk measures (duration, DV01, convexity), the risk-neutral drift in option pricing, and, for insurers, the fair value of both assets and liabilities.
Risk-free proxies. No asset is truly risk-free. Proxies are short-term rates anchored by central banks — government bills of top-rated sovereigns, and the new overnight benchmarks €STR (euro), SOFR (US), SONIA (UK), SARON (Switzerland), TONA (Japan) — and the derivatives written on them: futures, overnight indexed swaps (OIS). Risk-free rates are nominal: real rate plus expected inflation.

title: 9  Risk-free rates in practice
text:
9.2 Market conventions
Day counts. The year fraction \(\tau(t, T)\) between two dates depends on the day-count convention: ACT/360 (actual days divided by 360, standard for money markets), ACT/365, ACT/ACT, 30/360. For ACT/360, \(\tau(T_{i-1}, T_i) = (T_i - T_{i-1})/360\) with dates counted in days.
Business-day rules adjust payment dates falling on holidays: Following (next business day), Modified Following (next business day unless it crosses into the next month, then the previous one), Unadjusted.
Compounding. A ZCB price \(P(t, T)\) defines a spot rate in each convention:

Interpolation. Quotes exist only for some maturities, and are sparse or illiquid at the long end. Missing points are interpolated — linearly, by cubic splines, or with parametric families such as Nelson–Siegel. For par rates \(S_{T_{i-1}}, S_{T_i}\) quoted at consecutive maturities, linear interpolation gives, for \(T_{i-1} < T_h < T_i\), \[S_{T_h} = \frac{S_{T_{i-1}}(T_i - T_h) + S_{T_i}(T_h - T_{i-1})}{T_i - T_{i-1}} .\]
Bonds. A fixed-rate bond with coupon rate \(K\) and dates \(T_1, \dots, T_n\) is worth \[B_{fx}(t, T_n) = \sum_{i=1}^nP(t, T_i)\,\tau(T_{i-1}, T_i)\,K + P(t, T_n).\] For a defaultable issuer, market practice discounts with the risk-free zero rate plus a zero spread \(S\): with annual compounding \(\bar P(t, T) = (1 + R_a(t, T) + S)^{-\tau(t,T)}\), and the bond price uses \(\bar P\) in place of \(P\).

title: 9  Risk-free rates in practice
text:
9.3 From IBORs to RFRs
IBORs (Libor, Euribor) were for decades the benchmark for loans, notes and derivatives, and together with overnight rates (Fed Funds, EONIA) were treated as risk-free. During the 2007–2009 crisis the IBOR–overnight spread widened dramatically (Chapter 1), showing that IBORs contain bank credit and liquidity risk; IBOR quotes were also manipulated. Hence:

2013–2014: the Financial Stability Board reviews the major benchmarks and recommends alternatives;
2017: the UK FCA announces it will stop supporting Libor panels;
2019: ISDA establishes fallbacks to transaction-based overnight RFRs;
Libor is discontinued (USD Libor on 30 June 2023), replaced by SOFR, SONIA, SARON, TONA; in the euro area €STR replaced EONIA, while Euribor survives in reformed, transaction-based form.

The two kinds of rates differ structurally:

IBORs are forward-looking term rates: quoted for tenors from one week to one year as simple rates, fixed at the start of the accrual period — a market expectation.
RFRs are backward-looking overnight rates: published daily, with no term structure of their own; the rate for a period is obtained by compounding the daily fixings in arrears, so it is known only at the end of the period.

Correspondingly, three pricing environments have succeeded one another in a single currency:

Single curve, IBOR (before 2007): IBOR rates for both discounting and forwarding.
Dual curve (after 2007): overnight rates (EONIA, Fed Funds, now €STR, SOFR) for discounting, IBOR for forwarding — still the standard for Euribor derivatives.
Single curve, RFR, backward-looking: the RFR curve for both discounting and forwarding. This is the setting of the rest of the chapter.

title: 9  Risk-free rates in practice
text:
9.4 Backward-looking rates
Let \(C(t) = \exp\bigl(\int_0^tr(u)\,du\bigr)\) be the cash account driven by the instantaneous risk-free rate (Chapter 8), so that \(P(t, T) = \mathbb E^Q\bigl[e^{-\int_t^Tr(u)\,du}\bigm|\mathcal F_t\bigr]\).

For an accrual period \([T_{i-1}, T_i)\) with \(d_i\) business days, daily fixings \(r(i, j)\) and day-count fractions \(\delta(i, j)\), \[R(T_{i-1}, T_i) = \frac{1}{\tau(T_{i-1}, T_i)}\Bigl[\prod_{j=1}^{d_i}\bigl(1 + r(i, j)\delta(i, j)\bigr) - 1\Bigr] \;\approx\; \frac{1}{\tau(T_{i-1}, T_i)}\Bigl[\frac{C(T_i)}{C(T_{i-1})} - 1\Bigr],\] the continuous-time version being the limit of vanishing daily steps.


For \(t \leq T_{i-1}\), the expectation of \(R(T_{i-1}, T_i)\) under the \(T_i\)-forward measure (whose numeraire is \(P(\cdot, T_i)\)) is \[R(t, T_{i-1}, T_i) = \frac{1}{\tau(T_{i-1}, T_i)}\Bigl(\frac{P(t, T_{i-1})}{P(t, T_i)} - 1\Bigr),\] the same formula as the simple forward rate of the IBOR world. For \(T_{i-1} < t < T_i\) part of the rate is already known: \[R(t, T_{i-1}, T_i) = \frac{1}{\tau(T_{i-1}, T_i)}\Bigl(\frac{e^{\int_{T_{i-1}}^tr(u)\,du}}{P(t, T_i)} - 1\Bigr).\]

Proof. Under the \(T_i\)-forward measure, \(\mathbb E^{T_i}[X\mid\mathcal F_t] = \mathbb E^Q\bigl[e^{-\int_t^{T_i}r}X\bigm|\mathcal F_t\bigr]/P(t, T_i)\). With \(X = C(T_i)/C(T_{i-1})\), \(e^{-\int_t^{T_i}r}X = e^{-\int_t^{T_{i-1}}r}\), whose \(Q\)-expectation is \(P(t, T_{i-1})\). \(\square\)

9.4.1 Overnight indexed swaps
An OIS exchanges a fixed rate \(K\) against the compounded RFR. A payer OIS with floating dates \(T_1, \dots, T_n\), fixed dates \(T'_1, \dots, T'_m\) (same start and end), notional \(N\), valued at \(t < T_0\): \[OIS_R(t, T_0, T_n) = N\sum_{i=1}^nP(t, T_i)\tau(T_{i-1}, T_i)R(t, T_{i-1}, T_i) - N\sum_{j=1}^mP(t, T'_j)\tau(T'_{j-1}, T'_j)K .\] By the proposition, before the start this coincides with the single-curve Libor swap formula (and the floating leg telescopes to \(N(P(t, T_0) - P(t, T_n))\)). Once an accrual period has started, the known part of the compounded rate must be included: the first floating coupon becomes \(N\bigl(e^{\int_{T_0}^tr(u)\,du} - P(t, T_1)\bigr)\).


9.4.2 Swaptions
Assume the forward swap rate \(S_R(t, T_0, T_n)\) is a log-normal martingale under the swap (annuity) measure, with numeraire the annuity \(A(t) = \sum_jP(t, T'_j)\tau(T'_{j-1}, T'_j)\): \[\frac{dS_R(t, T_0, T_n)}{S_R(t, T_0, T_n)} = \sigma_S\,dW_t .\] Then the payer swaption follows Black’s (1976) formula \[PSWT_R(t) = N\,A(t)\bigl[S_R\Phi(d_1) - K\Phi(d_2)\bigr], \qquad d_{1,2} = \frac{\log(S_R/K) \pm \tfrac12\sigma_S^2(T_0 - t)}{\sigma_S\sqrt{T_0 - t}} .\] Swaption valuation is unaffected by whether the underlying floating rate is forward- or backward-looking: what matters is the swap rate at \(T_0\).


9.4.3 Caplets on backward-looking rates
A caplet on \([T_{i-1}, T_i]\) with strike \(K\) pays \(N\tau(T_{i-1}, T_i)\bigl(R(T_{i-1}, T_i) - K\bigr)^+\) at \(T_i\). The underlying rate keeps accruing during the period, so its uncertainty is resolved only at \(T_i\). Lyashenko and Mercurio (2019) model the forward rate as a log-normal martingale under the (extended) \(T_i\)-forward measure, with a volatility that decays linearly during the accrual period: \[\frac{dR(t, T_{i-1}, T_i)}{R(t, T_{i-1}, T_i)} = \sigma_R\min\Bigl(\frac{(T_i - t)^+}{T_i - T_{i-1}}, 1\Bigr)dW_t .\] (The extended ZCB price — the bond maturing at \(T_i\), with proceeds rolled over at the RFR after \(T_i\) — keeps the numeraire defined for \(t > T_i\).) This gives a Black formula \[CPLT_R(t) = N\tau(T_{i-1}, T_i)P(t, T_i)\bigl[R(t, T_{i-1}, T_i)\Phi(d_1) - K\Phi(d_2)\bigr], \qquad d_{1,2} = \frac{\log(R/K) \pm \tfrac12\Sigma_R^2}{\Sigma_R},\] with total variance \[\Sigma_R^2 = \sigma_R^2\int_t^{T_i}\min\Bigl(\frac{(T_i - s)^+}{T_i - T_{i-1}}, 1\Bigr)^2ds = \sigma_R^2\Bigl[\max(T_{i-1} - t, 0) + \frac{(T_i - \max(T_{i-1}, t))^3}{3(T_i - T_{i-1})^2}\Bigr].\] Since a forward-looking caplet’s rate is fixed at \(T_{i-1}\) (variance \(\sigma^2(T_{i-1} - t)\)), \(\Sigma_R \geq \Sigma_L\): the backward-looking caplet carries the extra variance of the accrual period, a third of its length.

On the curve bootstrapped below, the at-the-money caplet on \([1, 2]\) (forward rate \(3.407\%\)) with \(\sigma = 20\%\) is worth \(25.5\) bp of notional if the rate is forward-looking (\(\Sigma_L = 0.2\sqrt1\)) and \(29.4\) bp if backward-looking (\(\Sigma_R = 0.2\sqrt{1 + 1/3} = 0.231\)).

The same structure holds in the one- and two-factor Hull–White models, where the caplet becomes an option on \(C(T_i)/C(T_{i-1})\) and \(\Sigma_R^2\) splits into the variance of the bond’s forward price up to \(T_{i-1}\) plus the extra variance accumulated over \([T_{i-1}, T_i]\).

With an upward-sloping curve, zero rates lie slightly above par rates, and forward rates above both (the 1-year forward from 4 to 5 years is \(3.83\%\)).

In practice (e.g. SOFR on 30 September 2024) the procedure is the same with more instruments, real day counts, a few days’ spot lag and an interpolation scheme between pillars.

text:
9.7 Exercises

A deposit of 100 over 182 days pays 1.60 under ACT/360 simple interest. Find the simple rate and the equivalent continuously compounded rate under ACT/365.


Solution. \(\tau_{360} = 182/360 = 0.5056\), so \(R_s = 1.60/(100 \times 0.5056) = 3.165\%\). \(P = 1/1.016\); with \(\tau_{365} = 182/365 = 0.4986\), \(R_c = \log(1.016)/0.4986 = 3.184\%\).


Verify the bootstrap formula from the par condition and recompute \(P(0, 2)\) in the example.


Solution. At par, the floating leg \(1 - P(0, T_i)\) equals the fixed leg \(S_i\sum_{j\leq i}\tau_jP(0, T_j)\); isolating \(P(0, T_i)\) gives the formula. For \(T_2\): \(P(0, 2) = (1 - 0.032 \times 0.97087)/1.032 = 0.96893/1.032 = 0.93889\).


Compute the ratio \(\Sigma_R/\Sigma_L\) for a caplet on a 3-month period starting in 1 year, at \(t = 0\), and at \(t = T_{i-1} + 1.5\) months.


Solution. At \(t = 0\): \(\Sigma_R^2/\sigma^2 = 1 + 0.25/3 = 1.0833\) against \(\Sigma_L^2/\sigma^2 = 1\), ratio \(1.041\). Midway through the accrual period the forward-looking rate is already fixed (\(\Sigma_L = 0\)), while \(\Sigma_R^2/\sigma^2 = (0.125)^3/(3\times0.25^2) = 0.0104\): the backward-looking caplet still has optionality.


(Duration matching; Hull 4.11–4.12) An insurer must pay \(100\) in 10 years. The curve is flat at \(3\%\) (continuous). It can invest in 2-year and 30-year zero-coupon bonds. Find the holdings that match present value and duration, and explain why the hedge is not perfect.


Solution. The liability is worth \(L = 100e^{-0.3} = 74.08\) with duration \(10\). Holding present values \(x\) in the 2-year and \(y\) in the 30-year bond: \(x + y = 74.08\) and \(2x + 30y = 10 \times 74.08\), so \(y = 21.17\), \(x = 52.92\). The portfolio is immunised against small parallel shifts, and since its convexity (\(\frac{4x + 900y}{L} = 260\)) exceeds the liability’s (\(100\)), it gains from larger parallel moves. It remains exposed to non-parallel moves (a steepening of the curve between 10 and 30 years), and must be rebalanced as time passes and rates change, since durations drift.


(Hull 4.9) A deposit pays \(4\%\) per annum with continuous compounding, but interest is actually paid quarterly. How much interest is paid each quarter on \(10\,000\)?


Solution. The equivalent quarterly-compounded rate is \(4(e^{0.01} - 1) = 4.0201\%\), so each quarter pays \(10\,000 \times 0.040201/4 = 100.50\).

title: 10  FX options and automated market making
text:
10.1 FX options in brief
The previous chapters priced derivatives at their arbitrage-free “fair value”. A bank that trades with clients does something different: it makes a market, quoting a price at which it buys and a higher one at which it sells, and manages the risk left on its book. This chapter, based on a practitioner lecture by Veronika Lunina, describes how an automated market-making system for FX options works: valuation on the implied volatility surface, spreading, skewing, hedging, dealer intervention and system design. A short review of FX option pricing comes first.
An FX option is written on an exchange rate \(S_t\) (units of domestic currency per unit of foreign currency; for EURUSD, USD per EUR). Holding foreign currency earns the foreign interest rate \(r_f\), which acts like a continuous dividend yield. The Black–Scholes argument of Chapter 5 then gives the Garman–Kohlhagen formula: \[C = S_te^{-r_f(T-t)}\Phi(d_1) - Ke^{-r_d(T-t)}\Phi(d_2), \qquad d_{1,2} = \frac{\log(S_t/K) + (r_d - r_f \pm \tfrac12\sigma^2)(T - t)}{\sigma\sqrt{T - t}},\] with forward rate \(F_t = S_te^{(r_d - r_f)(T-t)}\) (covered interest parity). The spot Delta is \(e^{-r_f(T-t)}\Phi(d_1)\) and the vega \(S_te^{-r_f(T-t)}\varphi(d_1)\sqrt{T-t}\).
Prices are quoted in volatility. In the vanilla market, the price of an option is a vol: the number to plug into the Black–Scholes (Garman–Kohlhagen) formula, together with spot, rates and maturity, to obtain the premium in currency. The FX implied volatility surface shows a smile: at-the-money options have lower implied volatility than in- and out-of-the-money ones. By convention FX smiles are quoted in terms of Delta rather than strike — at-the-money, 25-delta and 10-delta risk reversals (call vol minus put vol, measuring skew) and butterflies (average wing vol minus ATM vol, measuring convexity).

title: 10  FX options and automated market making
text:
10.2 What is market making?
Market making means taking the opposite side of clients’ trades. A market maker does not take directional bets: it earns the bid–offer spread, selling at the offer and buying at the bid. Some asset classes are fully electronic (FX spot, cash equities); FX options are less liquid, with much volume still traded OTC and by “voice”. Because holding times are long in illiquid products, risk management is central.
Why automate? Quoting is time-consuming, and a human’s ability to quote while managing risk is limited. Quoting a £100m request takes as much effort as a £1m one, so a voice desk naturally neglects small trades. Automation lets a bank serve more clients and increase market share, providing liquidity on a scalable, 24/7 basis. It complements the trading desk; it does not replace it.

title: 10  FX options and automated market making
text:
10.4 Where is the mid?
The mid price is an abstraction: participants buy at offers and sell at bids, and the mid must be estimated. For vanillas it is read off the implied volatility surface: observed prices of the liquid points (ATM, risk reversals, butterflies at standard tenors) plus a model to interpolate between them give a mid vol for any strike and expiry. Determining the levels of the liquid points is called marking the surface; it is done by traders or automatically, for instance with a non-linear Kalman filter that updates the surface as new quotes and trades arrive. Exotic structures are valued with smile-consistent models (local-stochastic volatility, Chapter 7).

title: 10  FX options and automated market making
text:
10.6 Skewing
A market maker does not choose its trades: if client flow is one-sided, risk accumulates. Ideally the book stays “flat”. Risk can be reduced actively by executing hedges in the market — expensive, especially for vega in illiquid options — or passively by skewing: quoting tighter (closer to mid) on the side that would reduce the current risk, and wider on the side that would increase it. This raises the probability of favourable trades without paying to hedge.
Skewing needs a single quantitative measure of the book’s risk. For a Delta-hedged option book the main risks are vega (sensitivity to implied volatility, across tenors and strikes) and sensitivity to scheduled market events (central bank rate decisions, non-farm payrolls, …). With such a measure one computes the risk of the current portfolio, of the portfolio plus the trade and of the portfolio minus the trade, and makes the skew a function of these numbers: if buying the option from the client reduces risk, the bid moves up towards mid.

title: 10  FX options and automated market making
text:
10.7 Dealability and dealer intervention
The system has auto-dealable limits on trade size, depending on the currency pair, the option’s Delta, the time of day, and whether an event is under way. Requests outside the limits are re-routed to a human trader, who sees the prices suggested by the system and accepts or modifies them. Requests are also re-routed when anomalies are detected in the input market data or in the system’s outputs.

title: 10  FX options and automated market making
text:
10.8 System design
The system must be object-oriented and scalable: it supports different product types with possibly different spreading logic and is easy to extend to new products. Traders configure parameters that flow in as real-time inputs. Independent pieces of functionality are encapsulated in separate classes. Every price request, together with its market data and settings, can be serialised (saved as text) for testing and for investigating issues.

title: 10  FX options and automated market making
text:
10.10 Exercises

Show that the Garman–Kohlhagen formula follows from Black–Scholes by treating the foreign currency as an asset paying a continuous dividend yield \(r_f\).


Solution. One unit of foreign currency deposited abroad grows to \(e^{r_fT}\) units, worth \(S_Te^{r_fT}\) in domestic currency. The traded asset \(X_t = S_te^{r_ft}\) pays no dividends and, under the domestic risk-neutral measure, grows at \(r_d\); so \(S\) has risk-neutral drift \(r_d - r_f\). Repeating the Black–Scholes computation with \(\mathbb E^Q[S_T] = S_te^{(r_d - r_f)(T-t)}\) replaces \(S_t\) by \(S_te^{-r_f(T-t)}\) in the formula.


A desk is short 2m USD of vega (per vol point) in 1-year EURUSD. A client asks for a two-way price on a 1-year option with 20k USD vega per vol point. With a base spread of 0.2 vol each side, how should the quote be skewed?


Solution. Buying the option from the client (the client sells) would reduce the short vega position: the bank should improve its bid, e.g. quoting the bid only 0.1 vol below mid and the offer 0.3 vol above. The margin per side is roughly vega × spread: 2k USD on the bid side, 6k USD on the offer side.


(Hull 19.10) A bank has sold \(1000\) seven-month European calls on the yen (each on one yen). Spot \(0.80\) US cents per yen, strike \(0.81\), \(r_{USD} = 8\%\), \(r_{JPY} = 5\%\), volatility \(15\%\). Compute the Delta, Gamma, vega, Theta and rho of the position and interpret them.


Solution. With Garman–Kohlhagen, \(d_1 = 0.1016\), and per option (prices in cents): \(\Delta = e^{-r_fT}\Phi(d_1) = 0.525\), \(\Gamma = 4.206\), \(\mathcal V = 0.2355\) (per unit of volatility), \(\Theta = -0.0399\) per year, \(\rho = 0.223\) (per unit of \(r_{USD}\)). The short position has: Delta \(-525\) (the position loses \(5.25\) cents if the yen rises by \(0.01\) cent; hedge by buying 525 yen); Gamma \(-4206\) (Delta falls by \(4.2\) for each \(0.001\)-cent rise); vega \(-235.5\), i.e. \(-2.36\) cents per volatility point; Theta \(+39.9\) cents per year, i.e. about \(0.11\) cent per day earned by time decay; rho \(-223\), i.e. \(-2.23\) cents per percentage point of the US rate. Short options are short Gamma and vega and long Theta.
